In the case of higher-order functions,they are a specific type of function that accepts one or more functions as parameters and can also return a function as a result.

A key feature of Kotlin is that it treats functions as first-class citizens.This means higher-order functions are functions that can accept one or more functions as parameters,return them as re- sults,and even be stored in variables or passed around like any other value.However,this does not imply that every higher-order function is necessarily a pure function.

Higher-order functions build on the idea that functions in Kotlin are first-class citizens.In prac- tice,this means we can pass functions as arguments,return them as results,or assign them to variables.The benefit for a Java developer is that,instead of relying on static methods or utility classes,higher-order functions allow us to express behavior more directly and concisely.For ex- ample,operations on collections such as map,filter,or reduce let us declare what we want to achieve without having to write repetitive boilerplate code.This leads to cleaner,more reusable, and expressive programs.

Higher-order functions are commonly used in Kotlin to do the following:

* **Control data flow:**Pass different functions to a higher-order function to define specific behaviors at runtime.
* **Process collections:**reduce,filter,and map allow manipulating collections in a declarative way.
* **Dynamic functions:**By returning functions from other functions,we can generate custom behavior at runtime depending on the parameters.

Many of these operations are implemented as extension functions on collections.It is important to note that not all extension functions are higher-order functions;an extension function only qualifies as higher order ifit accepts or returns another function.For example,fun String.isEmail(): Boolean is a simple extension function,while fun <T>Iterable<T>.filter(predicate:(T) -Boolean)is both an extension function and a higher-order function.

Another useful clarification is that in Kotlin,we generally talk about functions,even when they are declared inside a class.However,when compiled to bytecode,they become methods from the perspective of Java.

All this is possible thanks to the ability to abstract behavior,compose functions,and build modular code capabilities that make higher-order functions such a central feature in Kotlin.

In this last section of the chapter,we are going to see something that will always be useful to us; in fact,it is something that we can always take advantage of if we are curious and want to see what is the same or different between Java and Kotlin.This topic is bytecode.

Bytecode is a code format that is generated after compiling a program written in a high-level language.In this case,both Kotlin and Java are languages that are considered high-level.

Another characteristic of bytecode is that it is code that is designed to be executed by a virtual machine,and we know that both Java and Kotlin use virtual machines.This is what allows by-tecode to be executed on any system that has a virtual machine that can read this code,that is, that can interpret it.

Java,especially in its early days,owes its growth and popularity to the use of bytecode,since it was a way of allowing software created with Java to be portable.By this,we mean that software created with Java could be executed on different operating systems thanks to the use of bytecode and a virtual machine compatible with the operating system found on the computer or device.

## Receivers

The concept of a receiver,as it exists in Kotlin,does not have a direct equivalent in Java.In Kotlin, a receiver is an object that provides a specific context within a function or lambda,allowing us to interact with its properties and methods directly,without needing to explicitly reference it (e.g.,using this).

It is important to note,however,that you can only interact with the properties and methods that are available at the correct access level.While the syntax may look as if the function is defined inside the class,a receiver(such as in extension functions)is essentially just syntax sugar and does not grant access to private members.

In Java,this concept is not directly available.While you can achieve similar behavior using meth- ods or passing objects explicitly,Java lacks the syntactic sugar provided by Kotlin's receivers.For example,in Kotlin,we can define extension functions or use lambdas with receivers,where the receiver becomes the implicit context within the block of code.This allows for more concise and readable code,as we can interact with the receiver object seamlessly within the function or lambda

A receiver in Kotlin establishes a context when we define it.By defining a receiver within a lambda or a function,the receiver can be accessed as if it were within the object.This helps us to avoid explicit references;therefore,we will have cleaner and less repetitive code,meaning we will be able to access the methods and properties as we normally do in objects,but without needing to use the name of the object or the word this.

## Collections in Java versus Kotlin

One of the fundamental differences between Java and Kotlin when it comes to handling collections lies in how they approach mutability.

In Java,all collections are inherently mutable,meaning that any code that has a reference to a collection can modify its contents.For example,when you pass List to a method in Java,that method always has the ability to modify the list,adding or removing elements,which can lead to unintended side effects and make code less predictable.

Kotlin,on the other hand,introduces a clear and explicit distinction between mutable and im-mutable collections.This separation is directly reflected in the type system,where List represents an immutable(read-only)collection and MutableList represents a collection that can be modified.

The difference becomes even more apparent in everyday practice.When working in Kotlin,you must make a conscious decision about the mutability of your collections.By default,factory func- tions such as listof()create immutable collections,while mutableListof()is used when you specifically need a collection that can be modified.This clarity in code intent not only improves security but also makes code easier to understand and maintain,as immutability by default re- duces the chance of bugs related to unintentional modifications of collections.

This explicit distinction of mutability in Kotlin reflects a more modern design philosophy that favors immutability by default,which is especially valuable in concurrent programming and long-term code maintenance.While in Java you would need to use additional constructs such as Collections.unmodifiableList()to achieve immutability,in Kotlin,this feature is built into the language naturally and efficiently.These are the options (immutables and mutables) we have available:

# Sequences

Sequences in Kotlin represent a significant evolution in collection handling,especially for de-
velopers coming from Java.While Java 8+introduced Streams as a way to process collections in
a lazy manner,Kotlin refined this concept with sequences,offering a more elegant and efficient
alternative.

Lazy evaluation is at the heart of sequences.This means that operations are not executed im-
mediately when they are declared,but only when they are needed.For a Java developer,this is
similar to how Streams work.The main difference is in how elements are processed:Java Streams
can batch or buffer elements depending on the operation (e.g.,sorted or distinct may need to
see multiple elements),while Kotlin sequences consistently process each element through the
entire chain of operations before moving on to the next.

For example,when you filter and transform a collection in Java using Streams,each intermediate
operation creates a new temporary collection.In contrast,Kotlin processes an element through
all operations before moving on to the next,significantly reducing memory usage and improving
performance,especially on large collections.

Another significant advantage is reusability.Unlike Java Streams,which can only be consumed

# Collections and Sequences

## Terminal operations

Terminal operations are operations performed at the end of a data pipeline,such as a Stream in Java or a sequence in Kotlin.These operations trigger the processing of all the elements in the stream or sequence-using them to produce a final result-and,as a result,the Stream or sequence is exhausted and cannot be reused for further processing.

Let's see common examples of terminal operations in Java:

`long count books.stream().count();/Total number of books`
**count():**Returns the number of elements in the stream:

`Optional<Book>firstBook books.stream().findFirst();`
**findFirst():**Finds the first element in the stream:

`List<Book>bookList books.stream().collect(Collectors.toList());`
**collect(Collectors.toList()):**Converts the stream to a list.

Now let's see how these operations would work in Kotlin.Here is the code:

`val count books.asSequence().count()//Total number of books`
**count():**Returns the number of elements in the sequence:

`val firstBook=books.asSequence().firstorNull()`
**firstorNull():**Finds the first element of the sequence,or returns null if it is empty:

`val bookList books.asSequence().toList()`
**toList():**Converts the sequence to a list.

The terminal operation triggers all processing in the order defined in the pipeline.

Terminal operations are crucial in processing Streams in Java and sequences in Kotlin,as they mark the end of the pipeline and consume the stream or sequence.In the case of Java Streams, once a terminal operation is executed,the Stream is consumed and cannot be reused.On the other hand,sequences in Kotlin allow data to be processed and then reused in new pipelines, offering greater flexibility.

These operations always produce a final result,which can vary depending on the purpose.For example,they can return a single value such as count or sum,generate a collection,such as with toList or collect,or simply perform a side effect,such as printing the elements with forEach. Their main purpose is to transform the stream or sequence into something tangible or useful.

# Chapter 10
269

Another key aspect of terminal operations is that they trigger the execution of all intermediate operations previously defined in the pipeline,such as filter or map.Until a terminal operation is invoked,these intermediate operations are not executed,especially in the case of sequences, where evaluation is lazy.

Finally,terminal operations end the processing of the pipeline.This means that,once executed, no more operations can be added to the stream (in Java)or to the processed sequence.This be- havior ensures that the pipeline has a clear end,producing the expected result after applying all the defined transformations.

## Advantages of sequences over Streams

Kotlin sequences have several advantages over Java Streams,making them more convenient and powerful in many use cases.One of the most obvious differences is Kotlin's more concise syntax. Thanks to higher-order functions and Kotlin's ability to work with lambdas natively,operations with sequences require less code and are more readable than their equivalents in Java Streams, where verbosity can be a disadvantage.

Another big advantage is that sequences in Kotlin can be converted to collections more directly.In Java Streams,when you want to transform a stream into a collection,you usually need to rely on the Collector utility (e.g.Collectors.toList());in Kotlin,it is enough to call toList(),which simplifies the conversion.Additionally,sequences benefit from the intuitive extension functions offered by Kotlin,such as filter,map,and take,which are built naturally into the language and allow for more expressive and consistent usage.

Sequences also have better integration with the Kotlin type system,allowing them to take ad- vantage of advanced features such as nullability interoperability.For example,while Streams return an Optional when working with possible null values,sequences simply use the Kotlin type system,returning null directly.This eliminates the need to handle additional containers such as Optional,and improves readability and data flow handling.

Here's when to use sequences:
* When you are working with large collections
* When you are working with chained operations
* When lazy processing is required
* When you need an infinite generation of elements

To simplify what a coroutine is,let's first look at the official definition:"A coroutine is an instance

is being cooked.

## Contexts and scope

Context and scope are fundamental concepts in the world of Kotlin coroutines and play a crucial role in managing their life cycle and behavior.

A context in Kotlin coroutines is like a container that groups key information about how and where a coroutine will run.This context includes the following:

- **Dispatcher:**Defines which thread or thread group the coroutine will run on,as follows:
    - Dispatchers.Io for I/O operations(such as working with files or network calls).
    - Dispatchers.Main for updating the UI.
- **Job:**Represents the specific task the coroutine performs.It also allows you to cancel it or monitor its progress.
- **Other attributes:**Can include things such as the following:
    - **CoroutineName:**A useful identifier to distinguish coroutines.
    - **NonCancellable:**Indicates that the coroutine should not be cancelled,even if its parent or associated scope is.

In addition,you can put custom elements into the coroutine context,such as an Mapped Diag-nostic Context(MDC)for logging.It is also important to remember that thread-local variables are not effective with coroutines,since a coroutine may resume on a different thread.If you need thread-local-like behavior,you should use ThreadContextElement to propagate context across suspensions.

In short,a coroutine's context sets up its execution environment:it defines where it runs,how it interacts with other processes,and what rules it should follow while working.It's like giving the coroutine a roadmap and tools to get it to perform its task correctly.

## Synchronous and asynchronous

Before diving into code,it's important to understand the fundamental difference between syn-
chronous and asynchronous execution.In synchronous programming,tasks are performed one
after another,and each step waits for the previous one to complete.In contrast,asynchronous
programming allows tasks to run independently or in parallel,enabling a program to remain
responsive while waiting for slower operations,such as network or database calls.

In this section,we'll explore these concepts through practical Kotlin examples.We'll see how
Kotlin handles both synchronous and asynchronous execution.

### What is synchronous programming?

Synchronous programming is very easy to describe.It is the execution of instructions or tasks in
a sequential manner,that is,we start at the beginning and finish at the end.

## Channels

Channels are a fundamental tool in Kotlin for communication between coroutines,offering a safe and efficient way to transfer streams of values between different pieces of asynchronous code. Strictly speaking,we can say that the definition of a channel is a flow of data that is sent and received between different coroutines.We could define it in a simpler way,as a means by which coroutines can communicate.

### Types of channels

We will start by describing the types of channels.For our examples,we will use the context of a delivery app.

#### Buffered channels

Buffered channels allow data to be temporarily stored in a buffer,decoupling the producer from the consumer.The buffer size is defined when the channel is created,allowing the producer to send multiple items without blocking,as long as the buffer is not full.The consumer,on the other hand,can process data at its own pace,drawing from the buffer as long as items are available, facilitating asynchronous coordination between both parties.

It is useful to us when there is a mismatch between the speed of the producer and the consumer. The advantage of using it is its flexibility and better handling of latency between tasks.

### Rendezvous channels

A rendezvous channel is not a different channel in theory from the unbuffered channel that we
just saw.We can say that rendezvous and unbuffered describe the same type of channel in Kotlin.
The origin of the term rendezvous comes from the ADA programming language used for con-
current programming;the name is in French and could be translated to something such as an
appointment or meeting.The main idea is that two processes must meet to achieve communi-
cation,and above all,it is related to the issue of synchronization that must be achieved between
the receiver and the sender.

Unbuffered can be said to be an easier term to understand for technical reasons,since the name
implies that it is a channel that does not have a buffer,and this name is also quite common in
telecommunications technologies,messages,and so on.

Although we are using the rendezvous channel here,it's helpful to explain it further in the context
of synchronization.Synchronization is a general concept in programming that ensures different
parts of a program coordinate their actions safely and predictably,just like how the rendezvous
channel forces the producer and consumer to meet at exactly the same moment.

## Pipeline

Now we will see a concept that is not a channel,but it is a concept closely related to channels
in Kotlin,and it is not exclusive to this language either.Pipeline is a design pattern that allows
data to be processed through a series of sequential stages,where each stage executes a specific
instruction or operation and passes the result of this to the next stage;hence,it is sequential.
In general,as mentioned,Pipeline is a design pattern within programming.It is not Kotlin-based,
so in other areas of computing,programming,operating systems,or software development,we
will also find this concept embedded.The Linux operating system is based on pipelines,where
you have a number of command-line tools.Each of them takes an input,performs some kind of
operation on this input,and creates new output.This output is then the input for the next stage
in a pipeline.

In Kotlin,technically,channels are the basis for the implementation of a pipeline.This is because
they are used as pipes that connect different stages of the process.Each stage of the pipeline will
produce and consume data using these channels,which in the end allows for concurrent and
efficient operations.

These are the stages into which we can divide the pipeline:

* producePackets:Generates the initial packets and sends them through a channel.

## Unit testing

When we talk about unit testing,we are talking about the most basic but essential processes
to ensure that our code works as we expect.Simply put,a unit test verifies that a specific piece
of your code(such as a function or method)does what it's supposed to do,regardless of what's
going on around it.It's like a magnifying glass that focuses on just one part of the code to make
sure it's built well before integrating it with everything else.

For example,if you have a function that adds two numbers,your unit test will confirm that 2+
3 always equals 5.It doesn't get complicated by external things,such as databases or services,
because those distractions aren't part of its job.

The following are characteristics of unit testing:
* Isolated:Each test is independent and does not depend on another.This makes them
reliable.
* Fast:Unit tests execute in milliseconds,which is ideal for running them every time you
make a change to your code.
* Deterministic:Tests give the same result every time,if the code does not change.

Unit testing is an essential tool for any developer looking to create robust and reliable software.
First,it helps you avoid unpleasant surprises by catching bugs before they reach production.
This not only improves the quality of the final product but also reduces the costs associated with
correcting problems later in development.Additionally,unit testing allows you to refactor with
confidence.When you decide to restructure your code,having a solid set oftests ensures that any

changes don't break existing functionality,acting as a safety net.Finally,unit tests serve as a form
of living documentation.Each test details how your code should behave under certain conditions,
making it not only easier for you to understand the system but also for other developers working
on the project.Writing unit tests is not just good practice;it is an investment in the stability and
maintainability of your software.

The following are quick tips for making useful unit tests:
* Give your tests clear names so it is obvious what they are checking.
* A test should focus on one thing.
* Use mocks when necessary,but don't abuse them.Keep tests simple and clear.

## Integration testing

Integration testing is as important to the testing process as unit testing;it is responsible for ver-
ifying how different components of a system work together,ensuring that they work correctly
when combined.Its scope includes testing entire business flows,validating interactions between
systems,and ensuring that the integration of individual parts meets established requirements.
These are some of the typical components that are tested in this type of testing:

* Databases
* External services
* APIs
* Filesystems
* Network components

## Differences between unit tests and integration tests

When writing automated tests,it's important to understand the different levels of testing and
what each one is intended to verify.Two common types are unit tests and integration tests,and
while they may seem similar at first glance,they serve very different purposes and involve dif-
ferent levels of complexity:

* **Complexity:**Integration tests are usually more complex to set up compared to unit tests.
This is because they require the preparation of multiple components or systems that must
work together.Additionally,they require more resources,such as databases,external
services,or realistic test environments.For this reason,its execution tends to be slower
and more demanding,both in time and computational capacity.On the other hand,unit
tests are much simpler,since they test a single component in isolation.This makes them
quick to run and easy to configure,making them an ideal tool for detecting small,specific
errors in a piece of code.
* **Scope:**The scope of both tests also varies considerably.Unit tests focus on validating
an individual component,verifying that it works correctly without depending on other
elements of the system.This ensures that each part of the code serves its specific purpose
independently.Instead,integration tests evaluate how multiple components interact
with each other.They validate entire business flows and ensure that parts of the system
work correctly together.This approach allows you to identify errors that may arise in the
interaction between modules or services,something that unit tests cannot detect.

# Domain-Specific Languages in Kotlin

## Understanding DSLs

A DSL is a computer language specialized for a particular application domain.Unlike a gener-
al-purpose language (GPL)such as Kotlin,Java,or Python,which is designed to solve a wide
array of problems,a DSL is tailored for a specific set of tasks or a particular domain.

There are generally two types of DSLs:

* **External DSLs:** These are languages parsed independently of the host GPL.They have
their own syntax,parser,and often,an interpreter or compiler.Examples include SQL
(for database queries),HTML (for web page structure),or regular expressions.Creating
external DSLs is a significant undertaking,requiring expertise in language design and
parsing technologies.Another example is how a Kotlin DSL is used for writing Gradle
configuration scripts.
* **Internal DSLs (or embedded DSLs):** These are created within an existing GPL.An internal
DSL is essentially a particular way of using the host language,leveraging its syntax and
features to create a more domain-specific API.The result is code that still compiles with
the host language's compiler but reads like a specialized language.This is the type of DSL
we will focus on in this chapter,using Kotlin as our host language.

Some of the most prominent advantages of using DSLs are as follows:

* **Improved readability and expressiveness:** DSLs allow you to express concepts in a way
that is natural to the problem domain,making the code easier to understand,even for
non-programmers or domain experts.
* **Increased productivity:** By providing high-level constructs tailored to the domain,DSLs
can reduce the amount of boilerplate code needed to perform common tasks.
* **Enhanced communication:** They can serve as a common language between developers
and domain experts,fostering better collaboration.
* **Domain focus:** DSLs help keep the focus on the what (the problem domain logic)rather
than the how (the low-level implementation details).
* **Type safety (for internal DSLs):** When built with a statically-typed language such as
Kotlin,internal DSLs benefit from compile-time checks,catching errors early.

ity,especially in a DSLbeing taught,the explicit author {..}and chapter {..}method
names are preferable.

### Benefits and trade-offs of our book DSL

The book DSL we created allows us to define a book,its authors,and its chapters.It does so in a
way that is very intuitive and concise.

The benefits are as follows:

* Readability:The DSL provides a clear,structured way to define book objects.The hierar-
chical nature mirrors the actual structure of a book.
* .Typesafety:Kotlin's compiler ensures that all parts of the DSLare used correctly(e.g,you
can't put a chapter block inside an authors block directly or assign a number to a title).
* Reduced boilerplate:Compare the DSLusage to manually creating Author objects,adding
them to ArrayLists,and then passing those to the Book constructor.The DSL is signifi-
cantly more concise.
* Maintainability:If the structure of the book or its components changes,the DSL build-
ers can be updated,and the compiler will help identify areas in the client code that need
adjustment.
* Discoverability(with IDE support):Kotlin IDEs offer excellent autocompletion.Within
a book {..}block,theIDEwill suggesttitle,numberofPages,authors {...)and
chapters {...)guiding the user.

There are certain trade-offs and considerations too:

* Initial development effort:Designing and implementing a DSL requires an upfront in-
vestment of time and thought.For very simple object creation,it might be overkill
* Learning curve:Users of the DSL need to understand its syntax and structure,though a
well-designed internal DSL should be intuitive.

372

# Domain-Specific Languages in Kotlin

* Complexity for simple cases:If you only ever create one or two books with minimal de-
tails,the DSL machinery might seem heavy.However,its benefits scale with complexity
and frequency of use.
* Potential for over-engineering:It's possible to create DSLs that are too complex or try to
be too"magical,"sacrificing clarity.The key is to find a balance that enhances readability
and productivity for the specific domain.

For our Book example,the DSL provides a clear win in terms of organizing complex object creation.

## Summary

Kotlin's powerful features,especially lambdas with receivers,make it an ideal language for craft-
ing internal domain-specific languages.By using the type-safe builder pattern,we can create
APIs that are not only expressive and readable but also benefit from Kotlin's static typing and
excellent IDE support.

In this chapter,we successfully built a DSL for defining Book objects.We saw how to structure
builders,use lambdas with receivers to create nested configurations,and provide a clean entry
point for the DSL.The resulting code for creating book instances is declarative,closely mirrors
the domain's structure,and is significantly cleaner than manual object instantiation.

# Kotlin for Java Developers

This book is a hands-on programming guide for Java developers who want to gain practical, production-ready knowledge of Kotlin.Whether you're maintaining Java systems or adopting Kotlin for Android,backend,or cross-platform projects,it will help you bridge the gap by building on your existing understanding of Java's syntax and design principles.

You'll begin by learning why Kotlin was created and how it improves on Java exploring types, expressions,control flow,and null handling while mapping each concept to familiar Java constructs. Each topic is introduced with clear purpose,showing how Kotlin's concise syntax,safety features,and expressive APls lead to cleaner,more maintainable code.

As you progress,you'll master object-oriented and functional programming,extension functions, smart casting,and interoperability with Java.The second half of the book dives into generics,data and sealed classes,coroutines for concurrency,and DSL design -demonstrating when and why to use these features to build scalable,elegant solutions.

By the end,you'll not only write idiomatic Kotlin but also understand the reasoning behind its design, enabling you to craft modern,reliable applications with confidence.

- Handle missing data safely with nullable types and safe calls

- Work with Kotlin collections and sequences to process data efficiently
- Use Kotlin with Java,Gradle,and Maven for seamless project builds

# Looking at the origin

Kotlin is a language that has taken a relevant role in the world of software development in recent years. It has been linked to the Java programming language since its inception, and this is because the developers who created it used Java as a starting point. They used the concepts of Java, Groovy, C#, and Scala. Kotlin uses many features that can be found in modern programming languages.

Kotlin was created by JetBrains, but it is also closely associated with Google, and this is because of Google's decision to make it its main language for the development of Android applications a few years ago.

The reality is that Kotlin was born within JetBrains, the company behind development tools such as Intellij IDEA, under the direction of Andrey Breslav. They decided to create a language that was completely interoperable with Java, but also, as we already mentioned, contained many modern language features. With the creation of Kotlin, they created a language that avoids being ambiguous, eliminates repetitive code, and increases the speed of coding while avoiding verbosity.

Kotlin was conceived in 2010 by JetBrains as a project to address the shortcomings of other languages used in its development tools, especially Java. The name Kotlin comes from the island of Kotlin, located near St. Petersburg.

In 2011, Kotlin was announced to the public. JetBrains decided to develop Kotlin openly from its initial stages, publishing its code on GitHub.

In 2016, Kotlin 1.0 was officially released, marking the first stable version of the language. This meant that JetBrains guaranteed forward compatibility, indicating that future versions would maintain compatibility with code written in Kotlin 1.0.

In 2017, Kotlin was introduced and mentioned for the first time at an official Google event – in this case, it was at Google I/O. This was done with a series of events around the world to present the advantages associated with Kotlin. But specifically, it was associated with the development of mobile applications on Android.

In 2019, two years later, Google shared it directly, pointing out that Kotlin would not only become an option within mobile development but would also become the primary option for Android application developers. This meant that the majority of tools, libraries, and other future elements that were going to be built for Android were considering Kotlin as the main language and thus being prepared in the best way to connect it to the projects.

Currently, mobile development is not Kotlin's only major focus. We find the possibility of using Kotlin in different departments of the software industry, such as the backend and some relatively new ones, such as blockchain. For example, in the case of the backend, it is increasingly common to find positions where the use of Kotlin with Spring is requested. This trend is growing, and in a short time, we will likely see other positions constantly requesting Kotlin as a default skill.

There is also Kotlin Multiplatform, allowing for the development of code that can be reused across different platforms.

In the well-known surveys that are done annually, such as the one on www.stackoverflow.com, we can see that Kotlin continues to grow and is one of the languages with the greatest acceptance, and that it has maintained this growth for a couple of years now.

# A quick review of Kotlin's popular features

Let's take a quick look of the main or most popular features that might be why Java developers decide to give the Kotlin programming language a chance:

- Null safety: Kotlin introduces a type system that distinguishes between references that can be null and those that cannot. This helps avoid NullPointerException errors, one of the most common errors in Java.

- Type inference: Kotlin has a strong type inference that reduces the need to explicitly specify the type of each variable, making the code cleaner and easier to read.   
- Extension functions: Extension functions allow you to add new functionality to existing classes without having to modify them or use patterns such as the decorator. This makes it easier to write cleaner, more maintainable code.   
- Lambda expressions: Kotlin enhances functional capabilities with lambda expressions with receivers, making it easier to create domain-specific languages (DSLs) and improve the functional use of the language.   
- Coroutines: Kotlin handles asynchronous programming and callbacks in a cleaner and less error-prone way by using coroutines, which allows asynchronous code to be written sequentially.   
- Data classes: Kotlin introduces data classes, which are very useful for classes that only serve to hold data. Data classes automatically derive methods such as equals(), hashCode(), and toString().   
- Delegated properties: Delegated properties allow you to delegate the logic of a property to a different object, facilitating certain design patterns and helping to reduce boilerplate code.   
- Smart casts: The Kotlin compiler can use smart casts, reducing the need for explicit casts in the code.   
- Improved flow control: Kotlin offers improved control flow structures, such as when and try-catch expressions that can return values.   
- $100\%$ interoperability with Java: Kotlin is fully interoperable with Java, allowing developers to use all existing Java libraries and frameworks in their Kotlin applications without problems.   
- Support for cross-platform development: With Kotlin Multiplatform, it is possible to write the logical core of applications and compile it for various platforms, such as iOS, Android, web, and servers, helping to share code and reduce development time. The main idea is to share business logic and other common components across different platforms while writing platform-specific code only when necessary.

As we have just seen, the list of popular features in Kotlin is extensive and will attract any developer interested in getting the most out of Kotlin. In our day-to-day projects, it is not necessary to master every single one of these features; in fact, it is not necessary to use them all. The reality is that the most important thing is simply to be aware of their existence so that when we face a challenge, we know which path to take or which options to consider to solve the problem.

If we used Kotlin in the backend, we would have the advantages of the learning curve. For example, Java is known for being a verbose programming language; in Kotlin, this learning curve is much shorter. On the other hand, there is also the issue of improvements in the code regarding the issue of null handling, which, as many Java developers know, is one of the main problems when we are working with Java.

Some of the main backend tools that you will find available to work with Kotlin are Spring and Ktor. Spring is one of the most famous Java frameworks, and you can find many projects and developers that already use it with Kotlin today. On the other hand, Ktor, which is a framework designed for Kotlin itself, is beginning to gain strength to work directly on the web with Kotlin as a backend language. Let's just remember that almost any tool that has current support and is used for Java could start using elements or parts of code completely in Kotlin.

# Kotlin/JS

Kotlin/JavaScript (Kotlin/JS) is a compiler that allows you to write web applications and server services using the Kotlin programming language. This means that using Kotlin, we can write the base code and then compile it to JavaScript. This feature is especially valuable for web developers who prefer a statically typed language, such as Kotlin, over JavaScript, which is dynamically typed.

# Note

1. Static typing: Data types are defined in the code and checked at compile time   
2. Dynamic typing: Data types are determined at runtime

Let's briefly explain how it works. Kotlin/JS takes the Kotlin source code and compiles it into pure JavaScript. This resulting JavaScript can run in any modern browser or in environments such as Node.js for server-side applications or tooling development.

Kotlin/JS offers complete interoperability with JavaScript libraries and frameworks. This is something that has surprised the community since you can call JavaScript code from Kotlin, and vice versa. This is made possible by type definitions that allow Kotlin to understand how to interact with JavaScript libraries.

Another of the main questions that JavaScript developers ask is whether Kotlin/JS supports a dynamic function that allows any part of the code to be treated as dynamic JavaScript, facilitating integration with JavaScript libraries that may not have well-defined types. The answer is yes.

Let's talk about some advantages of using Kotlin for this:

- Type safety: Kotlin offers compile-time type safety, which can help prevent many common errors in JavaScript related to data type, such as undefined properties.   
- Modern Kotlin features: Kotlin/JS allows developers to use all modern Kotlin features and coroutines.

We can give more details, but in reality, those are the two most important advantages, speaking specifically for the web. There are other advantages too, but they are more general and could apply to any development environment or application ecosystem.

# Kotlin for data analysis

Something that is not so well known is that we can use Kotlin for data analysis. This is not so well-known because other languages and tools have been around longer and are more popular, but Kotlin is starting to gain attention in this area.

# Kotlin and the Java Virtual Machine

Kotlin is a programming language that works on the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). In other words, this means that Kotlin needs a JVM installed on the device where we want our code to work. It is very common that when we start, we have many doubts about this, but later in this book, we will address the topic in detail.

Although Java is usually the language that is considered the one that had the most influence on the creation of Kotlin, there are also others, such as Scala, Groovy, and C#.

Kotlin is not the only programming language that uses the JVM. Although at present it may be the most popular, there are programming languages that have been doing it much longer, as shown here:

Groovy   
- Scala   
Clojure   
Jython

Fantom   
- Ruby

The concept is as simple as it is smart. A compiler compiles source code in any of these languages into a format called bytecode. The JVM then takes the bytecode and transforms it into machine-specific instructions.

As the bytecode is platform- and CPU-independent, this allows it to run on any platform where a JVM is available. This was called WORA back in the day, which stands for write once, run anywhere.

Knowing that Kotlin needs the JVM to function, we can say that the discussion around Kotlin being a language that wants to end Java loses a bit of meaning. On the contrary, we, as developers who work in such a fast and flexible industry, must learn to be open to changes but always respect technologies and languages, be attentive to true contributions, and not get carried away by sensationalist comments.

The portability that the JVM offers to all the languages that can work with it is a great advantage since you can use this to grow quickly, and you also do not have to rewrite the code for it to work on different platforms.

# Access modifiers

Java and Kotlin access modifiers are similar, but we must pay attention to some details. Access modifiers help us have control over the visibility of, and how to access, variables, classes, or methods. Depending on the needs of our programs, we can define the level of encapsulation and thus be able to ensure secure access to the data, both for reading and modifications.

As we already know, the Java modifiers are as follows:

public: The member is accessible from any other class.   
- private: The member is accessible only within the class in which it is declared.   
- protected: The member is accessible within its own class, by derived classes, and by other classes (same package).   
- default: The member is accessible only within classes of the same package.

In Kotlin, we have the following access modifiers:

public: The member is accessible from anywhere (as in Java).   
- private: The member is accessible only within the class or file in which it is declared (as in Java).   
- internal: The member is visible within the same module.   
- protected: This does not allow access from other classes in the same package, unlike Java, restricting it to subclasses only.

Another difference is that Kotlin does not have an equivalent of the default modifier. We could also say that Kotlin's internal access modifier is like Java's protected access modifier, but only accessible from the same class, child classes, and classes from the same module. The biggest difference between Java and Kotlin access modifiers lies in the scope of Kotlin's internal modifier, which provides module-level access control. This is in contrast to Java modifiers, which are limited to package, class, and subclass. This gives Kotlin greater flexibility in organizing and encapsulating code in multi-module applications.

A module is a set of Kotlin files that are compiled together. A module can contain source code, resources, and other files needed to build a part of the project. In other words, a module is a fundamental unit of organization and dependency management within a project. It encapsulates a set of related code, resources, and dependencies, promoting modularity and scalability for large projects.

Here is an example code in Kotlin applying the available access modifiers:

```kotlin
class Student(val name: String) {
    private val id = "AL0013670"
    internal fun printName() {
        println("Name: $name")
    }
} 
```

```txt
protected fun showId() { println("Id: $id") } } 
```

The following is an explanation of the code, focusing on the access modifiers:

The name property is a constructor parameter that is immutable by the word val, meaning that by assigning a value to name, we can no longer change it.   
The id property is set to private, which means that it can only be accessed from within the Student class. The value with which we initialize it is "AL0013670".   
The printName function is a function that is set as internal; this means that it will only be accessed within the same module in which this class resides. The function prints or displays the student's name.   
- The showId function is a protected function; this means that it can only be accessed within the same class or by classes that inherit from Student. This function is just used to print or display only the student ID.



# Important note

If we read the code carefully, we can see that we appear to be missing the public modifier. In Kotlin, if the access modifier is not placed, as is the case with name, then it is considered as the public modifier. So, this allows name to be accessed from anywhere.

The error would be as follows:


We will see that we no longer get an error, since with this change, we are allowing the variable of this type to be null as well. As mentioned, later, we will go deeper into this concept with more elaborate examples.

```txt
val name: String = ""
name = "Dimas";// Error: Val cannot be reassigned
```

As we can see in the last line of the preceding code, we will see an error, and this is simply due to the change we made from using var to now using val, as this does not allow the variable to change its value.

# Type inference

Kotlin supports type inference, meaning the compiler can help us assign a type to a variable, considering its initial value (that is, it infers the type we need). This helps us avoid having to specify the data type of the variable in some cases where initially there is a possibility that we do not know exactly what we are going to have, receive, or save.

This feature has existed since the beginning of the Kotlin language, so people who learned to program with Kotlin find it a natural feature. On the other hand, Java developers have worked without this feature for many years.

Starting with the Java 10 version, type inference is allowed. This is due to the introduction of the word var, and this instruction is what began to allow Java to also work with type inference.

This is how you define a variable in Kotlin with its type:

```txt
var name: String = "Noemi" 
```

We can see that we are indicating that the type is String. If we want Kotlin to infer the type, we remove the type that we explicitly placed:

```txt
var name = "Noemi" 
```

Both instructions do the same thing, creating a String type. In the first instruction, we are explicitly indicating that the variable will be of the String type, and in the second, we are letting Kotlin infer the type. The result in both is the same: we create a variable, name, that is a string.

In Java, starting with version 10, which we already mentioned, you can use var and infer the type. The Java code is very similar to that of Kotlin:

```txt
var name = "Viena" 
```

Something that we must highlight is that Java inference is mentioned as a limited inference. Type inference in Java is mostly limited to local variables and simple method parameters. In more complex cases, such as anonymous expressions or generics, explicit declarations are required. Kotlin offers a more powerful type inference that can handle instance variables, anonymous expressions, generics, lambdas, and more complex contexts, reducing the need for explicit declarations. In Java 10, some limitations of inference were presented. With the new versions, some features have been improved, but it is still known that Kotlin type inference is much more flexible. It can be considered a bit more precise if we compare it with Java.

Talking about inference in terms of the number of types, we can say that they have very similar basic elements. Kotlin treats Java's primitive types as objects; this makes it much simpler to work with the language.

Kotlin's type system is more flexible than Java's, not only because of type inference, but also due to its built-in support for nullable types and functional programming constructs. While Java relies on more explicit typing and primitive types, Kotlin allows developers to write more concise and expressive code. This may change with later versions of Java, but for now, this remains the case.

# Number

The Number type allows our variables to work with numeric values. Within Number, we have the following types:

- Byte: The range of values that can be stored in a Byte type is from -128 to 127. The size is 8 bits.   
- Short: The range of values that can be stored in a Short type is from -32768 to 32767. The size is 16 bits.   
- Int: The range of values that can be stored in an Int type is from -2147483648 to 2147483647. The size is 32 bits.   
- Long: The range of values that can be stored in a Long type is from -9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775807. The size is 64 bits.   
- Float: The range of values that can be stored in a Float type is from 1.4E-45 to 3.4028235E+38. The size is 32 bits.   
Double (64-bit): The range of values that can be stored in a Double type is from 4.9E-324 to 1.7976931348623157E+308. The size is 64 bits.

This is an example code of how to use the types that we have mentioned:

```txt
var byte: Byte = 10  
var short: Short = 100  
var integer: Int = 1000  
var long: Long = 10000  
var float: Float = 10000F  
var double: Double = 1000000.0 
```

In Kotlin, Java primitive types (all of them) are treated specially to maintain compatibility and efficiency. Kotlin does not explicitly distinguish between primitive types and their corresponding wrapper classes as in Java (e.g., Int vs. Integer). Unlike Java, which has separate primitive types and wrapper classes, Kotlin treats all data as objects. This simplifies code but raises a question: how does Kotlin maintain efficiency when targeting the JVM?

To answer this, Kotlin provides a simpler and more efficient way to work with data types. You write your code using objects, and the compiler intelligently handles the underlying representation (primitive or wrapper) for optimal performance and seamless JVM integration. This frees you from manual type management and allows you to focus on writing expressive and efficient Kotlin code.

To conclude, when we program in Kotlin, we don't need to worry about choosing between primitive types and wrapper objects like in Java, as Kotlin handles this transparently for us.

# Type checks (is and !is)

Kotlin, being a statically typed language, ensures type safety during development. This means that the compiler checks variable types at compile time to avoid errors at runtime. But there are situations where you may need to check or convert the type of an object. This is where type checking and conversions are used.

To verify, we have two instructions: is and !is.

This is an implementation example:

val name $=$ "Noemi" if(name is String){ print("String") }

If we execute this code, we will see the word "String" as a result because name is a string, and then the condition is true. We could also make an example with what would be a similar instruction, but with the! operator. This would be the code:

val name $=$ "Noemi" if(name!is String){ print("String") }

The difference is that, in this case, the condition is not met and, therefore, we will not execute the code found within the if condition. As we can see, this is a quick way to check the type of an object at runtime.

We are sure that the smart cast is being done in the first case, since upon entering the block, the compiler performs a smart cast from x(Any) to String, allowing you to directly access the length property of String without the need for an explicit cast.

In the second if condition, when it is verified that $x$ is of the Int type, and that block is entered, a smart cast is applied to Int. This allows you to use the inc() method, which is specific to integers (Int) in Kotlin, and increments the value by one.

The smart cast is effective here for the following reasons:

The $x$ variable is evaluated directly within the if blocks and is used immediately after- ward in a safe context.   
- $x$ is a local variable and not mutable (although, here, $x$ is passed as a parameter to the function; the context in each function call is independent, and $x$ does not change within each call.

This approach is safe and does not require explicit casting because the compiler can guarantee that the type of $x$ does not change between type checking and its use within each if block. However, if $x$ were a global variable or shared between multiple threads, then the smart cast might not be applied due to the potential for the value or type of $x$ to change in concurrent environments or between checks and uses.

Using smart cast simplifies code and improves readability, allowing you to write clearer and more concise code without the need for repetitive explicit casting.

# Unsafe cast operator and safe cast operator

When we talk about the unsafe conversion operator in Kotlin, we are talking about the as operator. This operator tries to explicitly convert a variable to a type that we indicate. If the conversion is not possible (since, as we know, some types are not compatible with each other), an exception will be thrown.

It is called unsafe since the operator, when making the conversion, does not verify whether the object can really be converted to the type that we have indicated. This ultimately generates an error, as we just mentioned, so the use of the word unsafe indicates the possibility of having an exception within our code. Here is an example:

```txt
var name: Any = 100  
val lastname: String = name as String 
```

This code in the editor will not show any errors, so as developers, we might be sure that it will work, but the reality is that it will not. If we execute this code, it will show us an exception that complies with what was mentioned previously. This cast is insecure due to the possibility of having an error, although at first glance, it seems that everything is fine with our code.

Here, we can make the code a little interesting by playing with the question mark, which, as we already mentioned, is used to work with nulls:

```txt
var name: Any = 100  
val lastname: String? = name as? String 
```

We have made the change so that the variable can now be a String type that has the possibility of accepting null:

```txt
val lastname: String? 
```

In addition, the as operator now also has the question mark, and thus we are protecting our code adequately against the failure of the conversion, which is why it is known as the safe cast operator. Here is an example:

```txt
name as? String 
```

If we execute the code, we'll see that it is working; the code will compile, but at runtime, the as? operator will fall because 100 cannot be converted to String. The value assigned to lastname will be null.

If we print lastname in this case, we will see that the result of printing it will be null. This is because when the cast is attempted and it is not possible, the value of null is assumed for that element.

In conclusion, we can say that the as operator is a great Kotlin tool if we understand what is happening in the code and the value. The recommendation is that if we don't know the type of value, we can use as? to avoid exceptions and make our code more secure.

# Interoperability, Gradle, and Maven

Transitioning from Java to Kotlin is not just a change in syntax but an evolution towards more modern and efficient programming. In this chapter, we will focus on three fundamental pillars for developers who want to integrate Kotlin into their existing projects or start new projects leveraging the Java ecosystem: interoperability, Gradle, and Maven.

One of Kotlin's greatest advantages is its seamless integration with existing Java code. This interoperability between Kotlin and Java is a game-changer for developers, enabling them to leverage the extensive ecosystem of Java libraries, frameworks, and tools without disruption. The interoperability feature allows for a hybrid code base where Kotlin and Java can coexist, interact, and complement each other efficiently. This capability ensures that developers can call methods, instantiate classes, and use Java libraries directly from Kotlin code, thereby preserving their established workflows and investments in Java infrastructure.

In the world of Kotlin/Java development, Gradle and Maven are indispensable tools for project management and dependency management. These build systems have been the backbone of Kotlin/Java projects, providing structured and automated ways to compile code, manage dependencies, and package applications. The good news for developers adopting Kotlin is that both Gradle and Maven are fully compatible with Kotlin, allowing for seamless integration into existing workflows and providing robust support for new Kotlin projects.

Gradle is a flexible and powerful build automation tool that has gained widespread adoption due to its performance and versatility. It uses a domain-specific language (DSL) based on Groovy or Kotlin to describe builds, offering a rich and expressive way to manage project configurations.

# Java Virtual Machine

The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) is a crucial component of the Java Runtime Environment (JRE) that enables Java applications to run on any device or operating system without modification. It abstracts away the underlying hardware and operating system, providing a uniform platform for Java bytecode execution.

To understand the importance of the JVM, we have to understand the concept of abstraction. This is key.

Abstraction allows developers to write code once and run it on any device or operating system that has a supported JVM, without requiring platform-specific modifications.

A simple example would be this: you are writing a Java application that needs to read and write files and modify directories in the file system. In a non-abstraction environment, you would have to worry about differences between operating systems, such as Windows, Linux, or macOS-specific commands for handling files.

The file system is different, and we would have a project in which we would have to change the instructions, the file writing methods, and the deleting methods, and all the instructions we use would have to be changed depending on the operating system. This would mean writing different code for each operating system. In short, we would have one problem in which we would have to program three solutions or variants of the code so that it adapts to the operating system where it will be executed.

This is where abstraction comes in. Thanks to abstraction, we don't have to worry about this.

The JVM is what provides this abstraction; we can use the same classes and methods of the standard Java API, and other instructions without worrying about the differences between the operating systems. The JVM is responsible for translating our calls to these methods into the specific operations of the underlying operating system.

# Benefits of abstraction

Let us now explore the advantages associated with abstraction:

- Portability: By abstracting hardware and operating system details, the JVM allows the same Java code to run on any platform that has a compatible JVM. This eliminates the need to rewrite or adjust code for different environments, which is a significant advantage for developers. The portability provided by the JVM means that applications can be developed on one platform and deployed on multiple platforms without any changes. This reduces development time and costs associated with creating and maintaining different versions of the same application for various operating systems. Additionally, it ensures consistency in application behavior across different environments, enhancing reliability and user experience.

- Simplification: Developers can focus on writing business logic and application functionality without worrying about the complexities of the underlying systems. The JVM handles the intricacies of interacting with the hardware and operating system, allowing developers to work at a higher level of abstraction. This simplification leads to cleaner, more understandable code, as developers do not need to include platform-specific hacks or workarounds. Furthermore, it reduces the margin of error by eliminating the need for developers to manage low-level details, which are often error-prone and can lead to bugs that are difficult to diagnose and fix.

- Maintenance: Abstraction makes code maintenance easier, as changes to the hardware or operating system do not require modifications to the Java code. The JVM is responsible for handling these differences internally, which means that updates or changes to the underlying platform do not affect the application code. This separation of concerns allows developers to focus on improving and extending the functionality of their applications rather than spending time on platform-specific adjustments. It also means that when new hardware or operating system versions are released, the JVM is updated to support them, ensuring that existing Java applications continue to run smoothly without requiring any code changes.

- Development efficiency: By providing a uniform platform, the JVM allows developers to reuse existing libraries and tools, speeding up development and improving efficiency. This uniformity means that developers can rely on a consistent set of APIs and tools across different projects, which reduces the learning curve and improves productivity. Additionally, the vast ecosystem of Java libraries and frameworks can be leveraged across various projects, enabling developers to build on proven solutions rather than reinventing the wheel. This reusability extends to development tools as well, such as IDEs, build systems, and testing frameworks, which all work seamlessly with the JVM. The result is a more streamlined and efficient development process, allowing developers to deliver high-quality software faster and with fewer resources.

The abstraction provided by the JVM offers numerous benefits that significantly enhance the development, deployment, and maintenance of Java applications. By ensuring portability, simplifying development, easing maintenance, and improving development efficiency, the JVM allows developers to create robust, high-performing applications that can run on a wide variety of platforms. This powerful abstraction layer is one of the key factors that has contributed to Java's enduring popularity and success in the software development industry.

# How the JVM achieves abstraction

The secret of the JVM is how it achieves abstraction through several sophisticated techniques, allowing it to provide a consistent execution environment on various hardware and operating systems for programmers. All these techniques ensure that Java applications can run smoothly on any platform if a compatible JVM is installed. Next, we'll delve a little more into the details of how the JVM achieves this.

# Just-in-time interpretation and compilation

The JVM interprets and/or compiles Java bytecode into system-specific machine code at runtime. This double approach guarantees flexibility and performance. Many times, programming languages in general are classified by languages that are interpreted or languages that are compiled. The languages that use the JVM have the characteristic that they can be interpreted and compiled:

- Interpretation: Initially, the JVM interprets the bytecode and executes it instruction by instruction. This allows immediate execution without the need for pre-Compilation into machine code. Interpretation is especially useful for code that runs infrequently.   
- Just-in-time compilation: For code that runs frequently, the JVM employs Just-in-time (JIT) compilation. The JIT compiler translates bytecode into native machine code at runtime, optimizing the code for specific hardware. This native code is then executed directly by the CPU, significantly improving performance. The JVM monitors which parts of the code are used most frequently and applies more aggressive optimizations to these hot spots.

# Standard Java API libraries

Standard Java API libraries play a crucial role in abstracting system-specific details. These libraries provide uniform interfaces for common tasks such as input/output operations, file manipulation, and networking:

- Consistent interfaces: Java API libraries provide consistent interfaces for developers, regardless of the underlying platform – for example, classes for file management, network connections, database connectors, and others. If we talk, for example, about the first case we mentioned of file management, then we are provided with methods for file operations that work in the same way on Windows, Linux, macOS, and other platforms. This would be the same for the other classes we mentioned.   
- Platform-specific implementations: At its core, the JVM includes platform-specific implementations of these libraries. When a Java application calls a method from the standard API, the JVM routes this call to the appropriate native implementation. This ensures that the same Java code can take advantage of the full capabilities of the underlying system without modification. We are not going to see this with the naked eye, but it happens.

# Resource management

Effective resource management is another key aspect of the JVM's abstraction capabilities. The JVM handles the allocation and release of resources such as memory and processes, optimizing these operations for any platform:

- Memory management: The JVM includes an automatic GC (we will explain it in the next section) that manages memory allocation and reclaiming. This GC runs in the background, identifying and freeing memory that is no longer in use. Different garbage collection algorithms are available (e.g., serial, parallel, CMS, G1, ZGC), each optimized for different use cases and system configurations.

- Process and thread management: The JVM abstracts the complexities of process and thread management. Java's threading model provides a high-level API for creating and managing threads, while the JVM maps these high-level threads to native operating system threads. This abstraction allows Java applications to take advantage of multicore processors and concurrent processing without having to deal with platform-specific threading complexities.

# The Java garbage collector

The garbage collector (GC) is a critical component of the JVM that automatically handles memory management for Java applications. Its main objective is to identify and free memory that is no longer being used by the program, preventing memory leaks, and optimizing resource use. Next, we will see details of how the GC works in Java, its different algorithms, and its impact on application performance.

The main goal of the GC is to manage memory efficiently to ensure that unused memory is reclaimed and that applications do not run out of memory. This is achieved by the following:

- Identification of unreachable objects: The GC tracks objects that no longer have active references in the program. These objects are considered unreachable, and their memory can be recycled, meaning it can be used for other elements.

Automatic memory release: Once unreachable objects are identified, the GC frees the memory they occupied, making it available for new allocations.

# Components of the GC

Memory management in Java is organized into several memory areas called generations, each optimized for different object types and usage patterns. The fundamental areas are as follows:

- Young Generation (on the heap): Stores young objects - those that have been created recently. Most of these objects are short-lived and are quickly collected by the GC. The Young Generation is further subdivided into the following:

- Eden Space (on the heap): Where new objects are initially created.   
- Survivor Spaces (on the heap): Two spaces where objects that survive the first collection in Eden are copied and evaluated again in future collections.

- Old Generation (Tenured Generation) (on the heap): Stores long-lived items that have survived multiple collections in the Young Generation. These items are rarer and are collected less often.   
- Permanent Generation (PermGen) (on the heap, up to Java 7): Stores metadata of classes and structures related to the JDK, such as class and method constants. In Java 8, this area has been replaced by Metaspace (outside the heap), which more efficiently manages this metadata outside of the main heap.

# Garbage collection algorithms

The JVM provides several garbage collection algorithms, each optimized for different usage scenarios and performance characteristics:

- Serial GC: Uses a single thread to perform garbage collection. It is simple and suitable for applications with small amounts of memory and fewer CPU cores.   
- Parallel GC: Uses multiple threads to perform collection in the Young Generation, improving performance in multi-core applications. It is efficient in systems with more processing capacity.   
- Concurrent Mark-Sweep (CMS) GC (Removed since Java 14): Performs most of its work concurrently with the application thread, reducing collection pauses. It is suitable for applications that require low latency, although it may be less efficient in terms of CPU usage.   
- Garbage-First (G1) GC: Designed for large applications. It divides the heap into regions and collects the ones that contain the most garbage first, providing a balance between performance and collection pauses. G1 is suitable for large server applications and has become the default GC in many recent versions of Java.   
Z Garbage Collector (ZGC) (Introduced in Java 11): ZGC is a low-latency GC designed to handle very large heaps, with minimal pause times. It's ideal for application responsiveness and tolerating minor trade-offs.

- Shenandoah GC (Introduced in Java 12): Low-latency GC, similar to ZGC, but focuses on concurrent collection. Reduces pause times regardless of the heap size by collecting garbage in parallel with the execution of application threads.

The garbage collection process usually goes through several essential phases to ensure efficient memory management in the JVM. These phases allow for identifying and freeing unused memory and optimizing memory organization for optimal performance. These phases are detailed next.

# Marking

The marking phase is the first stage in the garbage collection process. During this phase, the GC identifies all accessible (reachable) objects from the GC roots (such as local variables, stack registers, and static references). This process involves traversing the object graph, starting from these roots and marking each object that can be reached directly or indirectly. Objects that are marked are considered alive and in use. The objective is to determine which objects are still in use and, therefore, should not be collected. The collector uses a traversal algorithm to follow references and mark reachable objects. This phase can be expensive in terms of CPU time, especially in applications with large object graphs. Dial pauses can also affect application latency.

# Unmarking

Although it is not a formally recognized phase in all GC algorithms, umarking can be considered part of the post-collection cleanup process. In this phase, objects that are no longer in use (unreachable) are identified and unmarked. In some algorithms, this step involves preparing the memory occupied by these objects for reuse. The objective is to prepare unreachable objects to be collected and memory to be reused. The memory occupied by unchecked objects is put into a free memory list or directly recycled for new allocations. Ensure that all unreachable objects are correctly identified and unmarked without affecting live objects.

# Compaction

The compaction phase is essential to reduce memory fragmentation and create contiguous blocks of free memory. During this phase, objects in use move to occupy contiguous areas of memory, consolidating free space into one large block rather than many small chunks. This improves the efficiency of future memory allocations and can reduce the need for frequent garbage collection. The objects are moved to new locations, and all references to these objects are updated to reflect their new positions. This process can be complex, as it requires maintaining consistency of references during movement. Compaction can be a time-intensive process, especially in applications with enormous amounts of memory and many objects. Additionally, it requires longer pauses, which can affect application latency.

During garbage collection, pauses refer to the periods of time when the JVM stops the execution of application threads to perform memory cleanup tasks. These pauses are often referred to as stop-the-world events. Pauses can vary in duration depending on the garbage collection algorithm used and the size of the memory heap.

The GC is a crucial part of the JVM, although in reality, we could describe garbage collection as a process that works without us, and many developers know of its existence but not the details, as we have just explained. Now that we are analyzing how interoperability is crucial between Java and Kotlin, and we know that this is thanks to the JVM, it is good to know the details, and one of the most important and key elements is the GC.

The garbage collection process in Java is a series of phases meticulously designed to efficiently manage memory. From identifying and marking objects in use to memory compaction, each phase plays a crucial role in maintaining the performance and stability of Java applications. Understanding these phases allows developers to tune and optimize GC settings to meet the specific needs of their applications, balancing memory efficiency and overall system performance.

# Gradle and Maven

In today's software development world, we can see that tools appear every day to make programmers' lives easier. Many of them do not survive and simply become a fad for a year or a couple of years, if they are lucky, and then fade away.

In the world of software development with Java, we can say that the same thing happens in all languages. But some tools play an important role within the language, and the industry, and sometimes they stay for much longer. We can say that Gradle and Maven are examples of tools that have remained in the Java ecosystem for years and are probably the most used and well-known tools within the Java ecosystem.

Both tools have the main objective of being tools for project management. This can include tasks such as dependency management, as well as the automation of project construction or configuration.

There are more tools available, but these stand out due to their wide adoption. While they are often compared, they take different approaches to solving similar problems. Neither is inherently superior, and the choice depends on the specific situation and requirements.

We must remember that interoperability allows Kotlin to use many or most of the tools that are already being used in Java, which is why it is very common to find that the Kotlin market adopts the same tools or some slight variations.

# Maven

Out of the two options we have mentioned, Maven is the tool that has been on the market the longest, since it began to be used in 2004 and is now widely recognized. Being on the market for longer, it is clear that it has more information, more help, more forums, and a large community. It is also known for being a very well-documented and robust technology. With the time it has existed, implementations, and projects, we can say that the developer community also considers it to be very reliable.

Maven uses an XML-based approach to work. Its name is Project Object Model (POM). This is an XML file that defines the project model, which includes dependencies as well. This is a declarative structure.

There is a very popular principle in Maven, which is the convention over configuration principle. This means that a default structure is assumed and thus reduces the problem of having to configure the project.

Stability, as we mentioned, is not a problem for Maven, with the time it has been on the market, plus the community, it has a very clear focus and path to follow.

Finally, Maven integrates with what is known as a robust central repository, which facilitates dependency management.

To add Maven or Gradle to a project, it is best to do so during project creation. Typically, when creating a project, options for the project name, Java version, programming language, and the choice between Gradle or Maven are provided. This process is automated when using a wizard from the IDE. However, if you create the project manually, you will need to configure everything yourself. It is common practice to specify which build tool (Gradle or Maven) you will use at the start of the project.

There are more tools, but Maven and Gradle are the ones that dominate widely and stand out for the wide adoption they already have. # Decoding null in Kotlin

In the programming world, the concept of null values has been the cause of numerous errors and headaches. Null references have particularly been a critical source of bugs and crashes in Java, where the NPE is a common problem. Kotlin addresses this issue by incorporating null safety directly into the type system. In this section, we will explore how Kotlin handles nullability, ensuring that developers can write safer and more reliable code.

Before we discuss null from a Kotlin perspective, we will understand it from a Java perspective in order to later compare them. Let's look at the Java perspective of null.

# What is null in Java?

In Java, null is a value that represents the absence of an object. We could also say that null is a literal value that can be assigned to any reference type variable. Any reference of the type object can be null, meaning that it does not point to any instance of a particular object. However, using null in Java can be error-prone. The exception that occurs is an NPE, which occurs when you try to access methods or properties of an object that is null.

So, we can say that null is a value that can be assigned to any reference type variable.

At a technical level, we could say that when we have a null, it means that we have an object reference that does not point to any object in memory.

Each object in Java is stored in a memory region called the heap. When an object is created, a unique memory address is allocated on the heap, and this address is used to access the object. Reference variables do not directly contain the object but instead store the memory address where the object is located.

A null value is represented as a special address, called a null address, which does not point to any valid object in memory.

The null address is a special memory address used to indicate the absence of an object. In most computer architectures, this address is defined as a predefined constant value. Typically, the value $\theta$ is used, although in some architectures it may be -1 or some other specific value.

For example, in architectures such as those based on x86 processors, the memory address that represents null is implemented as the value 0. This means that if a memory address containing 0 is accessed, it is interpreted as a null reference.

In other architectures, such as those based on PowerPC processors, the null address may be implemented as the value -1. In this case, accessing a memory address containing -1 is interpreted as a null reference.
