Many times, when we talk about a feature of a programming language, we expect it to refer to just a character or a line of code. That is why when programmers are introduced to the concept of null safety, they are initially a little confused since it is not just one thing. Null safety is a concept encapsulating a set of characteristics of the programming language that are designed to prevent errors that can cause null references. These errors, as we are aware, are known as NPEs, and they occur at runtime.

Something we have already seen that we can include as part of null safety is the ability to have null and non-null types. It is very easy to distinguish whether we can have null by simply knowing the type, since if it is not of the nullable type, then we know that it cannot be null.

In Kotlin, the Elvis operator is a concise and convenient way to handle nullable variables and provide default values if they turn out to be null. It's represented by the question mark followed by a colon $(\text{?})$ .

The Elvis operator $(?:)$ provides a default value when an expression to its left is null.

```kotlin
}
```

```txt

```

The Elvis operator will return something; this something will be stored in the size variable, where we have two possibilities: if it is not null, then the first thing is executed, which is the instruction that is further to the left of where we ask for the size of name. But if the opposite is true, that is, if name is null, then we will execute the following instruction, which is then a text string that tells us that name is null.

As we can see, we can say simply that we already have a pre-made if ready to execute depending on the situation, whether it is null or not.

The Elvis operator is normally only used when we need to handle a value in a simple way. If we need to execute more than one instruction on a value or perform previous instructions a few more times, then the Elvis operator may be too short. In those cases, it would be recommended to use, as we saw previously, if that allows containing more complex operations in code and a large size. Another recommendation is to always think about whether there is the possibility of reducing the code by using this operator, since the simplicity achieved is very good and makes it easy to read.

Another situation where it is convenient to use the Elvis operator is if you want to provide a default value if the nullable variable is null.

We can compare the Elvis operator with the null-safe operator:

- Null-safe operator (?): Checks whether the variable is null before performing the operation. If null, it returns null.   
- Elvis operator (?): Provides a default value if the variable is null. If not null, it returns the variable's value.

Just as a gentle reminder, this and the other mechanisms for working with nulls we're looking at are part of null safety.

# Safe cast

To explain safe cast, we are going to use the code directly. This would be our example if we decided to use safe cast:

This line is the key part:

```txt

```

It performs a safe cast using the as? operator. This operator attempts to convert the value stored in name to a String type, but it does so safely:

- If name is null, or if it contains a value that cannot be converted to a string (e.g., an integer), the cast fails, and n will be assigned null. The as? operator prevents a ClassCastException error that would occur with an unsafe cast.

The as? operator allows for safe conversion of nullable variables, preventing crashes due to incompatible types or null values. Even though name is declared as Any?, the code attempts to convert it to a string using the safe cast. This is because the safe cast checks for compatibility before performing the conversion.

The safe cast operator (as?) in Kotlin is a valuable tool for working with types that may be null or unknown. It allows type conversions to be performed safely, returning null instead of throwing an exception if the conversion fails. This improves code robustness and clarity, making type handling safer and more predictable.

# What is an extension function?

Function extensions in Kotlin are one of the most interesting features in the universe of possibilities that Kotlin provides. We can say that a function extension will allow us to extend the functionality of a class that already exists. This highlights that function extensions allow us to increase the capabilities of the classes that we already have in our code so that we don't have to modify them.

Imagine going to a restaurant where the chef has already prepared a set menu with fixed dishes – pasta, pizza, and salads. You love the pasta but wish it came with a special sauce that's not on the menu. You can't ask the restaurant to change the pasta for everyone, but you can bring your own special sauce and pour it on top of your dish without changing the restaurant's menu. The pasta remains the same for other customers, but for you, it has an extra flavor because of the sauce you've added.

This is similar to Kotlin's extension functions: you can extend the behavior of a class (like adding the sauce to the pasta) without modifying the class itself. The class stays unchanged for everyone else, but you get the extra functionality that you need.

To return to code, the classes that we have defined in Kotlin can be extended with additional features or capabilities by using extension functions or extension properties. Extension functions allow developers to add new methods to existing classes without modifying their source code or inheriting from them, while extension properties provide a similar mechanism for adding new properties.

In this section, we will focus on extension functions, but it's worth noting that Kotlin offers extension properties as well, which allow you to add new fields or computed values to a class without altering its original structure.

It seems like simply adding something, but remember that we often use third-party classes or libraries that are closed to prevent certain actions. With extensions, we will have the ability to interact with them in a different way and not simply use them, but improve them and adapt them to our needs without much complexity.

This adheres to the open/closed principle: classes are open for extension, but closed to change. This is an important software design principle.

# How do function extensions work?

We need to make a few points clear, and we'll start with this one.

Extension functions in Kotlin don't actually modify the classes they are applied to. This means that they don't alter the original source code of the class. Instead, they provide new functionality to the class without altering its existing implementation.

Let's explain it in a more technical way so that we are $100\%$ clear about what happens in Kotlin. The Kotlin compiler transforms extension functions into static methods, passing the receiving object as the first argument. This means that there is no runtime overhead and the extended class is not actually modified. Kotlin generates static functions that take the receiver object as their first argument.

We already know this. However, we could say that extension functions promote modular code by allowing us to extend the functionality of a class without modifying its original source code, improving organization and readability. While extension functions enhance modularity, it's important to note that when extending third-party classes, the logic is not entirely in one place, as the original class and its extensions are defined in different locations. Despite this, extension functions maintain backward compatibility by not altering the original class directly.

Something we should be aware of is that when we name an extension function, there is a chance that it could share the same name as an existing method in the class. However, it's not just the name that matters – it's also the signature, which includes the receiver type and parameters. If the extension function has the same name and a matching signature as an existing method, the class method will take priority. This ensures that the class's base behavior remains intact. To avoid conflicts, it's important to review the class methods and their signatures and check the documentation to ensure that your extension function doesn't unintentionally clash with an existing method.

One important limitation of extension functions in Kotlin is that they can only access the public API of the class they are extending. This means that extension functions cannot directly access or modify private or protected members of the class. As a user, it's crucial to be aware of this restriction, as it limits the scope of what extension functions can do. They provide a convenient way to add new functionality, but their access is confined to what is already exposed by the class, ensuring that the internal implementation remains encapsulated and secure.

On the subject of visibility and the scope of extension functions, they can be declared at the file level, meaning they are not wrapped in a surrounding class. These functions can be placed in separate files to keep the code modular and organized. Declaring extension functions at the file level allows us to extend classes without modifying their source code and keep related extension functions together. This approach is especially useful when adding functionality to third-party or existing classes while keeping the extension logic separate from the rest of the code, improving maintainability and clarity.

As we already know, extension functions are compiled into static methods. This means that when we use extension functions, there is no additional performance overhead compared to regular functions. In fact, since they are compiled as static methods, their performance is comparable to that of regular static methods in Java. The key point is that extension functions do not introduce any extra runtime cost or slow down the execution of the program.

Even if we have full control over a class because we defined it ourselves, there are still valid reasons to use extension functions instead of regular member functions.

At first glance, it might seem unnecessary to define an extension when we could simply place the function inside the class as a method. However, Kotlin's extension functions offer several benefits that can make them a better choice in certain situations:

- Separation of concerns: Sometimes the behavior we want to implement does not belong to the core responsibilities of the class. By writing it as an extension, we keep the class clean and focused, while still providing additional functionality when needed.   
- Limited scope: Extension functions can be declared only in the modules or files where they are needed. This allows us to avoid overloading the class definition with functions that might not be useful globally.   
- Fluent APIs and DSLs: Extensions - especially when used with lambdas and receivers - can help us build more expressive APIs and domain-specific languages, which are harder to achieve with traditional methods inside a class.   
- Consistency with third-party or standard types: Even for classes we own, it's sometimes useful to offer functionality in the same way we do for external or standard library types (such as string, list, or date), maintaining a consistent extension-based API across our code base.

In conclusion, using an extension function even on a class we wrote ourselves is not just syntactic sugar. It's a deliberate design choice that can improve modularity, readability, and code organization.

If we look at the syntax, we can confirm that it is a function extension. Inside, we are indicating that the title value will change to The Best Java book, the author value will change to Dimas Lujan, and ISBN will change to 10000000.

At first, it seems like it is just a simple assignment, but there are several small advantages:

More concise and readable code   
Reduced repetition of the object name   
Useful for chain initialization

The apply function is an inline function, which means that the function's code is directly inserted at the call site during compilation, eliminating the need for a function call. This reduces the overhead at runtime and improves performance.

Not only do we have the ability to access the properties, but if we need to, we can also access the methods. If we need to change three properties of an object, we would have to write three separate instructions to access the three properties. We would have to use the name of the book followed by the name of the property (three times), so the code would become much smaller. Remember that we could find 10-20 objects in a normal code snippet, and each object could have 5-8 properties. This greatly increases the size of the code that we have, so we can achieve a lot of simplicity by simply knowing the capabilities that we have, thanks to Kotlin.

In a short and simple way, you can think of apply as an instruction that says "apply the following to the object and return the object once we have applied it." This is a powerful tool in Kotlin that allows you to write cleaner and more concise code, especially when it comes to setting up objects. Its ability to directly access object properties and methods, along with its return from the original object, makes it ideal for chain initializations and configurations.

# OOP overview

OOP is one of the most widely used programming paradigms to create software. You could also argue that it is the most popular, but it is certainly one of the many paradigms that all programmers must learn at some point, which is why we have dedicated a chapter to it in the book.

Some programming languages only support one programming paradigm, and others support more than one. A programming paradigm can be defined as a type of solution that is already defined, with some established ways of doing things, so when we use a programming paradigm, we use existing rules and definitions to try to address a type of problem and solve it in a certain way, or with a certain technique. It is a distinct set of concepts or thought patterns.

So, using a programming paradigm provides us with a foundational way of thinking about problems and structuring solutions in code. Each paradigm, such as object-oriented, functional, or procedural, comes with its own principles and abstractions. Understanding these paradigms helps

us approach problems more systematically and recognize how others have organized their code. While adapting a paradigm to a particular problem can be challenging, it guides us in identifying key components and designing solutions that align with well-established programming models.

Another issue is that, in the same software, we could use two or more paradigms for a solution. Of course, we would have to find a way to respect certain different rules, but it is possible. For example, a web page works with web technologies, but in the backend, the solution could use the object-oriented paradigm, so we would be using two paradigms, and more paradigms could be used if necessary.

Let's use a simple analogy. Two people can speak English, but one person speaks American English and the other British English. Both people speak the same language and can understand each other, but there are differences in accent, pronunciation and certain words. This is similar to paradigms; ultimately, the language is the same, but there are certain conventions that are different, depending on the paradigm. Additionally, certain technical aspects can increase the complexity of adapting our code to fit within the OOP paradigm. As a result, we can identify these challenges as inherent to the OOP approach.

Something we should remember in this chapter is that, in OOP, everything is an object.

# Classes

Although there is a lot to discuss about OOP, the word object stands out generally. However, the most important concept within OOP is probably the concept of classes because, without a class, we cannot have an object. But what is a class?

A class is the definition of an object. To achieve this definition, we must go through the process of abstraction. Abstraction is another of the most important concepts within OOP, since it is the process that allows us to know and better understand what an object is, and after the abstraction, we will then be able to create it.

Think of abstraction as trying to explain what a tiger is to someone who has never seen one. You wouldn't go into every tiny detail, such as how many whiskers a tiger has or the exact number of stripes. Instead, you'd focus on the main characteristics that make a tiger a tiger – it's a large, wild cat with orange fur and black stripes, sharp teeth, and it hunts for food. This process of identifying only the most important details and ignoring unnecessary ones is called abstraction. In programming, abstraction works the same way – we focus on the key features of an object or concept and leave out the details we don't need to deal with right now.

This process may seem obvious, but as programmers, we know that it is not. We don't all understand things in the same way, and that is why OOP is complex. Abstraction helps by abstracting the characteristics and actions that allow us to create the definition of a class, which becomes a vital process in OOP.

A class is simply the definition of the characteristics and actions that we want an object to have. Simply put, we could say that it is a block of code where we define where we will place the properties and actions that an object can have and perform when it is created. So, there has to be a class in order to create an object. A class is a blueprint for an object.

To create a class in Kotlin, the most common method is to create a file that refers to the class. For example, let's say we are going to create a file called Book; the extension of the file is .kt. However, this is still technically not a class; it is just a Kotlin file with the name Book. Inside the file, we will have to define what we want to be considered a class for use later, so inside the file, we will write the following:

```txt
class Book { } 
```

It doesn't make much sense to just create a class without any more code, but for this example, we will stick to the minimum, and we will increase the code depending on the concepts to explain. For now, the code is very clear – we place the word class to indicate that we want to create a class, which is followed by the name of the class, which is Book in this case. By convention, the first letter of the class name is capitalized (which is a rule in many programming languages) and should be singular. Then, we place the curly braces to indicate the code block of this Book class. Congratulations, you have defined your first class.

# Methods

When we refer to methods in OOP, what we mean is that they are the actions that an object can do. Just like properties, methods are defined within a class. By convention, properties are placed first and then the methods. Normally, actions are methods that are defined by name (such as run, jump, and read). These verbs help us get an idea of the action that is expected when the method is executed, such as read data or select database. You can provide parameters to methods if they require additional information in order to execute. On other occasions, those actions will return

a value, so we will have to be prepared to use that data. For now, we will define a method that simply prints the title of the book:

```kotlin

    var author:String = "Jose Lujan"
    var ISBN = "192838493"
    var pages = 250
    fun printTitle(){
        println("Book title: $title")
    }
} 
```

Methods and functions in programming share a close relationship. Both are blocks of code that can be invoked to perform a specific task or return a value. However, the main difference lies in their context. Functions are independent, meaning they don't necessarily belong to a class or object; they are more general and can exist on their own. On the other hand, methods are functions that are associated with a class or an object, and thus can only be called through an instance of that class (or directly through the class in the case of static methods). In short, every method is a function, but not every function is a method.

In Kotlin, functions are blocks of code that perform a specific task and can optionally return a value. To define a function, we use the fun keyword followed by the function name, parentheses for parameters, and braces for the body of the function.

When naming a function, if the name consists of two or more words, the words are written together, capitalizing the first letter of each word except the first one. This naming convention is called camel case. Examples are calculateTotal() and printMessage().

In this example, the printTitle method contains a simple print statement that outputs the title of the book. This method accesses the title property of the Book class and prints it. While it may seem as if calling the method gives you access to the property, it's important to note that it is the method itself that has access to the title property. This is because the method is part of the class and can interact with the class's internal properties. The caller of the printTitle function does not have direct access to the properties; the method does, and it performs the action of printing the property value.

# Unit and modifiers

Now, we will talk about two basic elements that help us understand Kotlin a little better when working with OOP: Unit and modifiers.

# Unit

A quick way to explain Unit to a Java developer is to say that it is similar to what we refer to as void in Java – that is, it represents the absence of a value when a function or method is returned. On a technical level, there are differences, although the fundamentals are the same.

We can see that all three methods now have a return value of Unit - the first two as Unit, and the last one, Int. It is generally not a good practice to explicitly use Unit as a return type in Kotlin, as it is inferred by default in functions that don't return a value. However, for functions with an expression body, it is very important to explicitly set the return type. This helps prevent accidentally changing the return type if the function's body is modified, ensuring that the intended return type remains consistent. We can simply take it as a rule that we must learn very soon in Kotlin: in the case of not placing a return value, Unit is used by default, even if it is not written explicitly.

Another piece of information that we should know is that although Unit is similar to void in Java, in Kotlin, Unit is considered a real type. Another interesting detail that is worth knowing is that void is not considered an object in Java, while in Kotlin, Unit is a singleton object. At a more technical level, Unit is compiled to Void in Java bytecode, and Unit is translated by Kotlin when it is called from Java, and void in Java is seen as Unit when it is called from Kotlin.

# Modifiers

We mentioned modifiers briefly previously in the book, and now, we will go into detail to explain them.

In Kotlin, we have four access modifiers that can be used in classes. They are as follows:

public   
- private   
protected   
- internal

Currently, everything we have in our code is public, since, by default, none of the properties have a modifier.

We are going to set pages and isRead as private. By doing so, we are going to limit access; only the elements within the class will have access:

```txt
private var pages = 250
private var isRead = false 
```

It's not only properties that can have modifiers; methods can too – for example, let's make the markAsRead method private:

private fun markAsRead(readDate:String){ this.isRead $=$ true this.readDate $=$ readDate }

With this change, markAsRead can only be accessed from within the Book class. This allows us to encapsulate data, ensuring that it cannot be manipulated from outside the class. This is called encapsulation or information hiding. Encapsulation is a key aspect of OOP that allows us to control access to certain properties or methods, thereby hiding the internal implementation details from code outside of the class.

Let's modify isbn to become protected:

```txt
protected var ISBN = "192838493" 
```

This allows access from the class where it is defined and from any subclass that inherits from it.

In simple words, isbn is accessible inside the Book class and in any class that inherits from Book. This is quite interesting and useful when, for example, we want some properties to be accessible according to their inheritance and not open to all elements in the code.

Now, we will modify author as internal:

```txt
internal var author:String = "Jose Lujan" 
```

By marking author as internal, the property is accessible from anywhere within the same module but not from outside of it. This means that code within the same module (for example, a set of related classes or files) can access and modify this property. However, it won't be accessible to code from other modules or libraries. Internal visibility sits between public (accessible from everywhere) and private (accessible only within the class or file), allowing for a balance between exposing functionality and maintaining some level of encapsulation.

- private: When we use this, we limit visibility to the class where the element is declared, so the properties or methods that use private are not accessible from outside the class.

# Kotlin constructors

The primary constructor is considered the main constructor when creating an object. It is called the primary constructor because it is the main or primary point where the object is initialized.

In Kotlin, the primary constructor is a constructor that is defined at the beginning of a class definition. Returning to our Book example, let's remember that the most basic way to define a class in the Kotlin programming language is as follows:

```txt
class Book { } 
```

If we want the properties we mentioned, we need to set them as follows:

```kotlin
class Book {
    var title:String = "Everything about Kotlin"
    var author:String = "Jose Lujan"
    var ISBN = "192838493"
    var pages = 250
    var isRead = false 
```

But first, we need to learn how to create our first object.

# Creating an object

To easily create an object in Kotlin, we will use the two files from our example, and to make things practical, we have not only the Book class (which we have already seen the code for, so we will not repeat it), but also the class where the program starts. This is the code:

fun main(){ val myBook:Book $=$ Book() println(myBook.title) }

We can see in the previous code that we have the main function that allows us to execute the code in Kotlin. We define the myBook object where we use the Book class to declare its type. We create the object as follows:

```kotlin
val myBook: Book = Book() 
```

We continue with the print instruction, simply to have something visual. If we review the Book code, we can see that the title of the book is Everything about Kotlin.

Congratulations! You have created your first object. When printing the title, we access myBook, and therefore, it is the object we have created. We can be sure that this object is present when we look at the output, which is the title of the book that we have placed in the class definition.

As in many programming languages, creating an object is referred to more elegantly as creating an instance of a class, the instance itself being the object.

It's worth remembering that the default constructor always has the name of the class and no input parameters.

# Primary constructor

Kotlin automatically generates a parameterless primary constructor (we can also call it a default constructor). We will use the same Book code as the starting point for the explanation of the primary constructor:

```kotlin
class Book {
    var title:String = "Everything about Kotlin"
    var author:String = "Jose Lujan"
    var ISBN = "192838493"
    var pages = 250
    var isRead = false 
```

This class has a default primary constructor. Although not explicitly written, Kotlin automatically generates a parameterless primary constructor.

The generated constructor would be equivalent to the following:

```kotlin
class Book constructor() { var title:String = "Everything about Kotlin" var author:String = "Jose Lujan" 
```

varISBN $\equiv$ "192838493" var pages $=$ 250 var isRead $=$ false

We can see that, after the word Book, which is the class name, we have the reserved word constructor, indicating that we are defining a constructor. By using the word constructor, we are explicitly telling Kotlin that we are defining a constructor. In this case, constructor() is the explicit declaration of the primary constructor without parameters. However, the constructor keyword is optional in this case and could be omitted, leaving simply Book() to define the primary constructor.

So, by having a primary constructor without parameters and actually following Kotlin's logic, there is not much point in placing the word constructor. We could omit it and allow Kotlin to do this work for us.

If you do not explicitly define a constructor in your class, Kotlin automatically generates a public parameterless constructor. This is what occurs in the background when no constructor is defined in the class.

Now, let's create a primary constructor. This is the code:

```javascript
class Book(var title: String, var author: String, var ISBN : String, var pages: Int, var isRead: Boolean){ 
```

We can see that we have removed several lines, including all of the property definitions. In Koltin, if we want to define a primary constructor, we can place the parameters directly inside the parentheses after the class name. This automatically creates properties and assigns them based on the values passed. In this example, we are using this approach to simplify the code by combining property declarations and the constructor. We have the title, author, ISBN, pages, and isRead properties listed inside the parentheses of the primary constructor. This indicates that when we create an object of the Book class, we will need to pass values for these properties in the constructor. We can also see in our code that, currently, the class has nothing. We simply open and close the brace, but we have no code inside it, so we have the class defined, and it only has one primary constructor.

Now, let's see how to create an object and use the constructor:

```kotlin
fun main() { val myBook: Book = Book( "The best Kotlin Book", "Jose Lujan", "192839ND39431", 250, false ) println(myBook.title) } 
```

In our main function, we are creating the myBook object using a primary constructor. When we create the object, we need to pass the five parameters that were specified in the constructor. This is because we have not defined another constructor, and we only have this constructor to work with, so we place the values that we are going to need.

This type of constructor can be a little confusing at first for developers who come from Java (specifically, it is the definition that is made in the code), but over time, they will be able to adapt and realize the benefit of reducing code and making it easier to define.

We are not finished with this primary constructor yet. If you come from the Java world, you'd know that it is common for a constructor to contain not only an assigned value that arrives through parameters. We also need, on some occasions, to perform extra operations to be able to assign values; they can be calculations, query operations, and so on. The type of operation is not important, but it is important to execute more complex instructions that are not only an assignment. In these cases, we must ask the question: how can we use code in a primary constructor?

The answer to this is very simple; let's look at the code:

```kotlin
class Book(var title: String, var author: String, var ISBN : String, var pages: Int, var isRead: Boolean){ init { title = title uppercase() author = author uppercase() println("Created Book: $title by $author") } } 
```

In the preceding code, we see the definition of the primary constructor with the five parameters: title, author, ISBN, pages, and isRead. To execute additional code during the initialization of the object, we use the init block. The init block is called every time an instance of the class is created, and it's useful for executing any setup or logic that needs to happen when the object is initialized.

For example, in our case, we are converting the title and author properties to uppercase using the uppercase() function. After performing this transformation, we print the modified values to verify the changes.

It's important to note that the init block is executed after the primary constructor, which means you can use or modify the properties initialized by the primary constructor. However, the init block is not suitable for defining new variables or properties. If you need to initialize additional variables, it should be done in the constructor or by defining them as properties of the class.

The init block in Kotlin is used to execute initialization code when an instance of a class is created. It is a special block that runs immediately after the primary constructor has been called, and it is useful for performing additional setup or initializations that cannot be handled directly in the constructor.

Examples of when to use the init block are as follows:

- Validating or transforming values passed to the constructor.   
- Executing code that depends on all properties initialized by the constructor.   
- Printing messages or performing tasks that need to happen every time an object of the class is created.

One important point is that you cannot declare new properties inside the init block; its purpose is to work with properties that have already been defined and initialized by the constructor.

Then, we will rely on init to place code, and thus, the primary constructor can have instructions that we need to execute when initializing an object.

Something that is important to mention here is that we can have multiple init blocks in code. It is possible to have multiple init blocks within the same class. All init blocks are executed in the order in which they appear in the code, immediately after the primary constructor has initialized the class properties.

# What are generics?

Let's start by discussing what generics are. As the name suggests, something that is generic implies that we will have "something" that is defined in a general way, and we can use it depending on certain situations or characteristics.

The idea of defining something as generic has the advantage of making it more flexible and reusable. The principle behind this is straightforward: when we design our code to handle only specific types, we limit its applicability. However, by allowing more general type parameters, we expand the range of possibilities and make our code adaptable to different types and scenarios.

At first glance, we could say that generics is a concept that we normally find in programming when playing with the parameterization of types. But let's apply a more technical definition to understand the concept better - generics is a feature that can be applied to programming languages, in general, to define and use types/methods with non-specific types so that, later, during their compilation or execution, they are used in a specific way.

This may seem simple, but it is not. Many factors need to be considered, such as the interoperability of certain types and performance concerns related to the execution time of specific tasks. For instance, using generics with complex data structures can sometimes lead to overhead during type checking or when dealing with type erasure at runtime. Additionally, operations involving generic collections or type casting might introduce subtle performance costs that can impact the efficiency of critical sections of code.

A key question to ask when working with generics is: what do we want to achieve with them? Generics in Kotlin enable you to define classes, interfaces, and functions that can operate with a variety of data types while maintaining type safety. This flexibility allows for more reusable and adaptable code, which can be tailored to specific types during compilation or execution.

When we use generics with functions, we can see their main benefit: the code we write becomes more adaptable and can work with different types. For properties, generics allow us to handle values of various types, making our code more flexible and capable of supporting different use cases.

We can see that, in general, what we are looking for is flexibility, reusability, adaptation, expanding options, and adjusting to different situations.

# Key concept - inline and reified types in Kotlin

When we mark a function as inline in Kotlin, the compiler copies the body of the function to each place where it is called, rather than creating an actual function call. This mechanism allows the use of reified types. By using reified with a generic type in an inline function, you instruct the compiler to retain type information during compilation. This enables type-specific operations that would not be possible with regular generics due to type erasure.

Now, we are ready to place the options inside when; we have already explained the modifications and what happens with inline and reified. This is the code:

```txt
inline fun <reified T> printItem(item: T) where T: Number, T:Comparable<T>{ when(T::class){ Int::class -> println("Integer") Float::class -> println("Float") else -> println("Unknown") } } 
```

We have three paths that can be taken in our case; when we have an integer, we will print a string indicating it. All paths print something.

We also consider Float, and print the text "Float". Finally, we have an else case if there is anything else we want to print as unknown.

The implementation of inline and reified is not a major problem; the important thing is simply to understand the reason why we are using them.

What we wanted to know was what reified is; now we know it.

reified is a powerful feature in Kotlin that allows you to work with generic types at runtime, overcoming the limitations of type erasure. It is especially useful when we need to perform operations that depend on the exact type of the generic parameter. However, this feature comes with its limitations: reified types can only be used within inline functions, and inline functions should be used thoughtfully, as inlining increases the size of the generated bytecode and may impact performance if overused.

In summary, using reified types with inline functions allows type checking at runtime, which is not possible with standard generics. This is particularly useful when we need to dynamically check whether an item is of a compatible type, as it enables operations involving reflection or type checking at runtime. However, it is important to note that reified types can only be used within inline functions, which have their own restrictions. inline functions should be used with care, as inlining increases the size of the compiled code and may affect performance. Therefore, reified types should not always be seen as a substitute for basic generics.

# Variance

We are approaching the final part of this chapter We will now discuss variance and other concepts that are related to it.

Variance in Kotlin is an important concept when working with generics.

Variance helps us understand how generics relate to inheritance and how values can be assigned from one type to another. It refers to the way generics behave with respect to inheritance and type relationships.

Concretely, variance determines whether a generic type can be replaced by another generic type. This then helps us understand and manage the possible or incompatible types in generics and other elements, where there is an inheritance relationship between types.

If we want to give a slightly more formal definition, we could say that variance refers to the relationship of generic types and the relationship of subtypes between type parameters.

When approaching the topic of variance, there are three new concepts that we have to understand; these concepts describe the aforementioned relationships:

Invariance   
Covariance (out)   
- Contravariance (in)

The fundamental problem here is that if we allowed generics to be variants by default, the following could happen:

We could end up with type violations at runtime.   
We would lose the type safety that is one of the main advantages of strongly typed languages.

To address the need to manage the relationship between generic types and inheritance, the concepts of covariance and contravariance were introduced. Covariance, denoted by out, allows mappings from more specific types to more general types and is useful when only reading data. On the other hand, contravariance, denoted by in, allows mappings from more general types to more specific types and is useful when only writing data. These concepts help to manage type relationships safely in different scenarios.

# Invariance

By default, generic types are invariant in Kotlin.

Invariance refers to a property of generic types in Kotlin (and other programming languages) where a type parameter does not allow for subtype substitution. This means that when a type is invariant, one cannot use a type with a different generic type, even if there is a parent-child relationship between them.

In simpler terms, if a certain type is defined as invariant, it is treated strictly as that specific type and cannot be automatically replaced with a more specific or more general type. This ensures type safety by preventing potentially unsafe assignments, but it also limits flexibility when working with related types.

In Kotlin, generics are invariant by default, so an invariant type can only be used with the exact type it was defined with.

Let's suppose we have four different types. Figure will be the main class, or the parent class of everything. We will then have three more classes that are child classes of Figure. The classes are Triangle, Circle, and Square.

# Plain Old Java Object (POJO)

In Java, there are no data classes; in fact, this is a concept introduced by Kotlin and appears only in this programming language.

In Java, the concept of a Plain Old Java Object (POJO) originated to describe simple objects that do not depend on third-party frameworks or libraries.

A POJO is simply a Java class that has no dependencies on any frameworks. The term was coined to contrast with classes that required inheriting from specific framework classes or implementing special interfaces.

The following are characteristics of a POJO:

It is framework-independent.   
It has no special restrictions on its structure.   
It is not required to follow specific conventions.   
It can have any constructor.   
Fields can be public or private.   
It is not required to implement any specific method.

# JavaBeans

A JavaBean is a class that follows specific design conventions.

JavaBeans can commonly be confused with POJOs. POJO is simply a framework-agnostic class that does not rely on predefined structures or annotations. To clarify the distinction from POJOs, the following conventions are typical for JavaBeans:

- A JavaBean does not extend from predefined classes, only from an object.   
It has no framework annotations.   
It does not implement predefined interfaces.   
Properties should be private to encapsulate the data.   
Getters and setters are public since they are the way to access and modify properties.   
JavaBeans should have the implementation of the equals, hashCode and toString methods.

POJOs are more flexible and lightweight, suitable for modeling data without any imposed rules, while JavaBeans are designed to integrate with tools and frameworks that rely on these conventions, such as Java EE, serialization libraries, or data mapping. In short, JavaBeans are a more structured and standardized form of POJOs, geared toward scenarios where interoperability and tooling are essential.

# Sealed classes

Unlike many, this concept is very easy to explain since we can summarize it in very few words, and it is easy to understand. Sealed classes are used to represent restricted class hierarchies.

If we want to give a more detailed explanation, we can say that sealed classes allow us to represent limited data types through a restricted hierarchy of classes. We can also use them to represent states.

We can explain sealed classes in two ways for Java developers. For developers using Java versions prior to Java 15, the concept might seem somewhat similar to enums, as both can represent a restricted set of types. However, they are fundamentally different: enums are singleton objects that represent a single state, while sealed classes can define hierarchies of objects or classes. In Kotlin, we also have enums, and we will cover them later. In this chapter, we will not compare the concepts. For developers who have worked with Java version 15 or higher, it is possible that you will know the concept of sealed classes already, as Java introduced this feature as a preview in version 15 and made it a standard part of the language in Java 17. While the idea is similar between Java and Kotlin, the implementation details differ slightly.

Moving forward, let's try to understand the concept of a closed hierarchy to deepen the explanation.

A closed hierarchy can be defined by the characteristic that all its subclasses must be known at compile time. This allows the compiler to perform exhaustive checks, which is especially useful in when expressions.

To declare a sealed class, we will have to declare a class using the sealed and class keywords. Take the following example:

sealed class Book

Another element to consider is that all direct subclasses must be declared in the same file as the sealed class. But in addition, the subclasses can be simple classes like any other that we define, without anything special, just using the word class. They can also be data classes or object classes.

Something important to remember is that sealed classes are implicitly abstract, so we don't need to use the word abstract in their definition; they are abstract by default. Additionally, like any other class in Kotlin, sealed classes are public by default unless a different visibility modifier is specified. You can change their visibility as needed, using the same syntax as for other elements in Kotlin.

Here, we see several benefits of using sealed classes:

- Flexibility: Each book, for example, can have its own unique properties and behaviors.   
- Expressiveness: The code is clearly structured, showing the relationships between different types of books. However, it's important to consider that if the hierarchy becomes too deep or the classes grow large, the code might become harder to read and maintain. However, sealed classes go a step further by enforcing that all subclasses are explicitly handled in when expressions. This way of working allows us to have the code ready to work with some design patterns; for example, a design pattern that could be easily implemented with this way of working is the State pattern.

# Sealed interfaces

In Kotlin, sealed interfaces give us the ability to define a limited set of implementations, as with sealed classes, but with the advantage of focusing on behavior rather than shared state or properties. This is ideal for organizing type hierarchies that rely more on actions than common data.

For example, let's say we're still on the topic of books and we're working on a book management system where user roles with the following profiles have different access levels: administrator, guest, and registered user. This is where sealed interfaces come into their own, as they allow us to model these differences in a clear, controlled, and secure way.

Here's how they work and what they benefit from:

- Controlled hierarchies: All classes or objects that implement a sealed interface must be declared in the same file or, depending on the version of Kotlin you're using, within the same package. This restriction ensures that the compiler has complete knowledge of all possible implementations, allowing for greater code security and clarity.   
- Exhaustive checking in when: A major benefit of sealed interfaces is their integration with when expressions. When you use a when expression with a sealed interface, the compiler makes sure that all implementations are accounted for. If you forget to handle one, the compiler will show you an error, helping you prevent runtime crashes.   
- Flexibility with multiple inheritance: Unlike sealed classes, sealed interfaces allow a class to implement multiple interfaces. This makes them an ideal tool for modeling shared behavior in complex systems, where a class may need to inherit functionality from multiple sources.

In short, sealed interfaces combine the advantages of controlled hierarchies with the flexibility of multiple inheritance, making them a perfect choice for structuring behavior-focused systems while ensuring that the code is robust and maintainable. Let's look at some code for more details:

sealed interfaceUserRole   
objectAdmin:UserRole{ fun addBook(title:String,author:String){ println("Book $\mathbb{S}$ title'by\$author added.） }

We can see that this code defines a handleUserRole function that handles actions of a user (user) based on their role (UserRole) and the type of action (action). It uses an exhaustive when expression to check the role:

Admin: Can add or delete books   
Editor: Can edit book details   
- Reader: Can read books

If we decide to add a new role, the compiler will force us to update this when expression, ensuring that everything is covered.

Sealed interfaces and sealed classes have key differences that make them suitable for different scenarios. Sealed interfaces allow multiple inheritance, making them an ideal choice for modeling shared behaviors across types. In contrast, sealed classes do not support multiple inheritance but are better suited for handling complex hierarchies that combine both state and behavior. While sealed interfaces focus on representing behavior-focused hierarchies, sealed classes are more useful when you need to work with defined data and state.

In summary, sealed interfaces are a powerful tool in Kotlin that, although similar to sealed classes, stand out when we want to model behavior-based hierarchies in a flexible and controlled way.

# Enumer

Enumer are one of the most popular concepts within programming. They are not very difficult to explain or understand, and they are widely used when programming systems that have a complexity above what we can consider as something basic.

In general, the definition of an enum is that it is a special type of data that represents a fixed set of values. That is, we have a list of possible and unique values for a type of variable. A classic example of this is the days of the week (Monday, Tuesday...) but why use an enum instead of constants? Enums provide several advantages over constants: they are type-safe, ensuring that only valid values are used; they group related constants into a single type, making the code more organized and readable; and they can include additional properties or methods, adding more functionality compared to plain constants.

We know that the days, for example, do not change, and if we use them within a program, we could manage them in a fixed way; this would be a great example of the use of an enum. Other classic examples are the months of the year and the cardinal points.

In Kotlin, we can say that an enum is a special class since it represents a set of constant elements. In fact, as we mentioned, enum is a general programming concept, but an enum in Kotlin is different from what we normally know. In fact, if we compare it with enums in Java, we will confirm that it is different. One of the important features of enums in Kotlin, similar to Java, is that they are instances of the Enum class itself, so they can also have properties and methods.

This is important because we can associate specific data or behavior with each enum value. For example, we can define methods in the Enum class that all enum constants will share, but it also allows for methods to provide customized functionality for specific constants. However, it's essential to note that this customization applies to the enum as a whole, not to individual values with their own methods. Enums are not typically used for abstraction; their primary purpose is to represent a restricted set of constant values in a clear and type-safe manner. By leveraging their features, we can write more expressive and structured code.

To explain more details, we will use this code:

```kotlin

    SUNDAY(false);
    fun isWeekend() = !isWorkday
    companion object {
        fun getWorkdays() = values().filter { it.isWorkday }
    }
} 
```

To define an enum, we use the word enum before the word class as we have in the first line of this code. Then, we define a value that will tell us if that day is a workday. This is just to add a little detail to the example:

name:This property returns the name of the enum constant as a string.

# Sealed classes and enums

In Kotlin, we have two options for representing controlled sets of values: sealed classes and enums. Sealed classes are more flexible because they allow us to define subclasses, each with unique properties and methods. This makes them ideal for modeling complex states or hierarchies, where each state can have its own behavior or additional data. On the other hand, enums are better suited for simpler scenarios where we need a predefined and limited set of constant values, all of the same type. Enums are typically used to represent different states of an entity, such as the days of the week or traffic light colors, or the status of an order. They provide type safety and clarity without the complexity of sealed classes.

Another feature is that enums are serializable by default and we can use an implementation of equals and hashCode. We must not forget that although all these elements are available by default, we could overwrite them if we need different behavior in some situations, although it is not common to do so.

# What is functional programming?

In Chapter 5, the focus was on object-oriented programming. In this chapter, it will be on functional programming. We will also investigate other concepts to understand and be able to use the related concepts.

Functional programming is a programming paradigm that treats computation as the evaluation of functions. It avoids changes in state and mutable data. The programming that we normally use is different. It is known as imperative programming, and it does just the opposite; its emphasis is on changes in the state of the program.

Something that we must always remember when we are trying to understand functional programming is that this programming paradigm focuses on "what" we are doing. If we use the opposite approach, which would be the imperative one, we would then be focused on "how" we are doing it.

Probably one of the key details of functional programming that stands out to programmers is that traditional cyclic instructions are discouraged. In other words, constructs such as for, while, and do while loops are generally not used. Depending on the language, there may be alternatives, but the common approach in functional programming is to replace cycles with recursion or higher-order functions. This is quite significant, as since the inception of programming, these cycles have been among the most used and taught topics.

If we wanted to relate Java and functional programming, we could say that the most important change came with Java 8, where three crucial elements were introduced that gave Java the capacity to support the functional paradigm. These three elements were as follows:

- Lambda   
- Streams   
Functional interfaces

Something important to mention is that Java is not a pure functional programming language, and this made the implementation of functional programming a bit verbose. Tail recursion optimization is not a possible implementation in Java due to its limited immutability. For this and other reasons, Java programmers had to do a bit more work if they wanted to apply this paradigm, unlike pure functional programming languages. But this did not stop the adoption of the functional paradigm in the Java community; it began to be used and is still being implemented. # Immutability

Immutability is probably the easiest principle to explain. As the name suggests, the idea is that data should not change after it is created. We know that data can change during the execution of programs, but the idea here changes a bit since instead of modifying existing data, new data is then created. This seems very simple and even unnecessary, but if applied well, it can reduce many errors since the possibility of the state being modified in an unexpected or incorrect way in other parts of the software is reduced.

The use of immutable variables and data structures is promoted when working with functional programming languages.

As we already know, in Kotlin, we have two possibilities when declaring variables: one is to declare immutable variables and another is to declare mutable variables. # Purity

Purity in programming – it sounds a bit strange, but to explain it better, we will use the concept of pure functions. When we talk about purity or pure functions, we are saying that these functions must have these important elements:

It should be deterministic. This means a function must always return the same result for the same arguments, no matter how many times we execute it.   
- No external state should be modified. In other words, we should not change global variables, databases, or any other external data source. It is also important to note that if a pure function calls a non-pure function, then the calling function itself is no longer pure.   
- No external state should be modified. In other words, we should not change global variables, databases, or any other external data source. It is also important to note that if a pure function calls a non-pure function, then the calling function itself is no longer pure. In simple words, a pure function should only have one effect: returning a value.   
- Here, it is useful to distinguish between external state modification and side effects. External state modification is one kind of side effect, referring specifically to changing something outside the function, such as a global variable or a database record. Side effects, however, cover a broader range of behaviors, such as printing to the console, throwing exceptions, or reading the current time. This distinction helps clarify why purity is stricter than just avoiding changes to the external state.

Now, we are going to see the concepts in code to understand them better. A pure function is as follows:

```autohotkey
fun add(a:Int, b:Int): Int {
return a + b
} 
```

In the preceding code, we can see that we have defined a pure function. It is easy to see this because the add function always returns the same result for the two elements that are received. If we set $a = 10$ and $b = 1$ , it always returns 11, regardless of what is happening; it will always be 11.

Another element that we already explained and that doesn't have side effects is easy to notice, as we see the function does not change the global state of anything.

Finally, we do not perform any external operation; we only take the two arguments that we have, which are a and b, and return the result of the operation without modifying anything else.

With this, we can then confirm that the add function that we have defined can be considered a completely pure function.

To make clear the subject of what a side effect is, we are going to demonstrate with code. A side effect occurs when a function interacts with what we can consider external context or the outside world. In simple terms, this can be the modification of the external state, such as updating

a global variable, changing a database record, writing to a file, or mutating an object that exists outside the scope of the function. Remember that in a pure function, this should not happen. All we expect in a pure function is that everything happens within the function and depends only on its parameters. Of course, it can also return a value, which is considered the output of the function, but all within its scope and context. This is the code of a function with side effects; we can also say that it is a non-pure function:

var result $= 0$ fun add(a:Int){ result $+ = 1$

Now, we can see that the add function is modifying the result variable. If this result variable is outside the function, then the behavior of the add function is dependent on an external factor. This results in the function not being considered pure.

Understanding what makes a function pure and identifying pure functions in code, as we have discussed previously, is relatively straightforward. A pure function is one that, given the same input, will always produce the same output without causing or depending on any side effects (such as modifying a global state). This predictability is one of its greatest benefits. With pure functions, you can always be certain of their behavior, which eliminates the need to track changes in external states or worry about unexpected side effects.

Another advantage is the ease with which tests can be done since we do not need to prepare anything special. As you'll remember, we focus only on the function and do not depend on external states. Finally, another advantage is that models modularize the code in a simple way; we have isolated code that is completely functional just by passing parameters and waiting for some output, so we can modularize most of the code without problems.

# Higher-order functions

In Kotlin, functions are treated as first-class citizens. This means they can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, returned as values, or even stored in data structures. Building on this property, higher-order functions are simply functions that either take other functions as parameters or return them as results. This close relationship makes it easier to understand higher-order functions as a natural consequence of treating functions as first-class citizens.

In simpler terms, functions as first-class citizens is the general principle that allows functions to be stored in variables, returned as results, or passed around like any other value. Higher-order functions are a specific use of this principle: they are functions that either take other functions as parameters or return them as results. In other words, higher-order functions are possible because functions are first-class citizens.

While this may remind us of the idea that functions are first-class citizens, it's important to clarify that we're not just referring to passing functions around; we're also highlighting how they can be returned, stored, and manipulated like any other value in Kotlin.

The concepts of functions as first-class citizens and higher-order functions are very closely related. However, there are differences that we must be aware of.

In the case of functions as first-class citizens, remember that the following apply:

They are assigned to variables.   
They are passed as arguments to other functions.   
They are returned from functions.   
They are stored in data structures.

In short, this implies that functions will be treated as values or first-class objects.

In the case of higher-order functions, they are a specific type of function that accepts one or more functions as parameters and can also return a function as a result.

A key feature of Kotlin is that it treats functions as first-class citizens. This means higher-order functions are functions that can accept one or more functions as parameters, return them as results, and even be stored in variables or passed around like any other value. However, this does not imply that every higher-order function is necessarily a pure function.

Higher-order functions build on the idea that functions in Kotlin are first-class citizens. In practice, this means we can pass functions as arguments, return them as results, or assign them to variables. The benefit for a Java developer is that, instead of relying on static methods or utility classes, higher-order functions allow us to express behavior more directly and concisely. For example, operations on collections such as map, filter, or reduce let us declare what we want to achieve without having to write repetitive boilerplate code. This leads to cleaner, more reusable, and expressive programs.

In simpler terms, we can summarize it as follows – not all first-class citizen functions are of a higher order, but all higher-order functions are treated as first-class functions, since they manipulate functions as values.

This is an example of a higher-order function:

fun operate(a:Int,b:Int,operation:(Int,Int) -> Int):Int{ return operation(a,b)   
}   
val sum $=$ operate(10,1){x,y->x+y}   
val product $=$ operate(10,1){x,y->x\*y}

As we can see, the operate function is a higher-order function because it receives another function as a parameter, named operation. This means that operate can take any function that matches the required signature as an argument, making it a flexible and reusable tool for various operations.

In summary, higher-order functions are a powerful tool within functional programming that allow us to write very expressive code. In fact, Kotlin can very efficiently handle collections thanks to higher-order functions. Some of the most common operations are reduce, map, and filter.

Higher-order functions are commonly used in Kotlin to do the following:

- Control data flow: Pass different functions to a higher-order function to define specific behaviors at runtime.   
- Process collections: reduce, filter, and map allow manipulating collections in a declarative way.   
- Dynamic functions: By returning functions from other functions, we can generate custom behavior at runtime depending on the parameters.

Many of these operations are implemented as extension functions on collections. It is important to note that not all extension functions are higher-order functions; an extension function only qualifies as higher order if it accepts or returns another function. For example, fun String.isEmail(): Boolean is a simple extension function, while fun <T> iterable<T>.filterpredicate: (T) -> Boolean) is both an extension function and a higher-order function.

Another useful clarification is that in Kotlin, we generally talk about functions, even when they are declared inside a class. However, when compiled to bytecode, they become methods from the perspective of Java.

All this is possible thanks to the ability to abstract behavior, compose functions, and build modular code capabilities that make higher-order functions such a central feature in Kotlin.

# Inline functions

If we are talking about functional programming in Kotlin and higher-order functions, it is inevitable that we will talk about inline functions in Kotlin. The "inline" concept means that the body of the function is placed directly in the place where it is called; that is, a new function instance is not created at each invocation. Explaining it in another way, we could say that an inline function is one whose body is going to be copied right to the space where it is called at compile time. For that, we will have to use the word inline in the function declaration.

So, instead of calling the function, the compiler removes that call and inserts the code of the function itself at that point.

This is an example of code for an inline function:

```kotlin
inline fun operate(a: Int, b:Int, operation: (Int, Int) -> Int): Int{ return operation(a,b)   
}   
val sum = operate(10,1){ x, y -> x + y }   
val product = operate(10,1){ x, y -> x *y } 
```

Let's walk through the code. In the first line, we can see how this function is now inline. This is because we have placed the inline reserved word at the beginning of the function, before the word fun.

This means that instead of making a call to the operate function during execution, the compiler will replace each call to operate with the body of the function and the provided lambda.

We have already seen the same function previously without inline, so now we will describe the difference between with and without inline:

- Without inline, the compiler will have to generate an object for the lambda $-\{x, y \rightarrow x + y\}$ and pass it to the operate function.   
- With inline, the compiler will insert the body of the function and the lambda directly into the part of the code where the function is called, thus eliminating the need to create the lambda object or make a call to the function.

When we use inline, we can find these improvements:

- We improve performance. Since inline functions indicate a copy and paste of the body, we are eliminating the creation of function objects and calls to the function. Therefore, there are blocks or functions to be executed.

It reduces the overhead of lambdas. In Kotlin, when we use lambdas, an object is created that is passed directly to the function. So, if we use inline, this object is no longer created since we are using inline to place it in the place of the call.

There aren't just advantages to using inline; everything comes at a price. So, we need to know when it is convenient or not to use inline.

Using inline functions is sure to increase the size of the bytecode. Although the size will vary, remember that if the function is called many times, the body will then be copied and pasted in all those places where the function is called. If the code for that function is large, then the bytecode will also be large.

You should not always use inline. A misconception is that it is a great option and so it should always be used. The reality is that the performance benefit is what should dictate whether or not we use inline. We have to consider the number of calls and the size of the code that will be added. This is the only thing that will tell us if it is really an improvement for our code.

To help, we can pose the explanation as a question: when do we use inline functions?

If we have small functions, it is a good option, since they do not have much code.   
If we frequently call functions, then the benefit can also be positive.   
- If we have lambda functions, it could also be a good idea to use inline, since they are usually small, and performance is important in them.

# The noinline function

Continuing with Kotlin and the context of functional programming, when we declare a function as inline, we already know that the function's body and its associated lambda parameters are inlined at the call site; in other words, their code is copied directly into the calling function. However, this behavior might not always be suitable for every parameter or every scenario we face. In some cases, we may not want certain parameters to be inlined. For such situations, Kotlin provides specific mechanisms to exclude parameters from being inlined.

We can say that no inline is a modifier used in inline function parameters to indicate that a specific function parameter should not be made inline.

Let's go back to the previous example where we created an inline function. Now we will use noinline as well. This is the code:

```kotlin

```

```txt
return operation(a,b) 
```

We can see in the code that the main function, which is operate, is still inline as before, but there is a change. This change is in operation. In operation, we place the noinline instruction before the parameter that we want to ensure is not inline. What this will mean for Kotlin is that the function itself will be inlined, but the lambda operation will not be inlined. In other words, it is treated as it is normally treated.

Among the important considerations when we want to use inline are the following:

We can only use noinline in function parameters that are already clearly marked as inline.   
- noinline will help us reduce the size of the bytecode if a lambda is used many times within a large inline function.

The use of inline and noinline is key to having precise control over what we are doing. Combining them allows us to optimize the code in terms of performance improvement in a great way. The important thing is to keep learning and using them to notice and analyze the differences in their use in different situations. This will never be easy, and even less so when we first begin to use them. Only with practice can we learn and understand in which cases it is better or not to apply them.

# Receivers

The concept of a receiver, as it exists in Kotlin, does not have a direct equivalent in Java. In Kotlin, a receiver is an object that provides a specific context within a function or lambda, allowing us to interact with its properties and methods directly, without needing to explicitly reference it (e.g., using this).

It is important to note, however, that you can only interact with the properties and methods that are available at the correct access level. While the syntax may look as if the function is defined inside the class, a receiver (such as in extension functions) is essentially just syntax sugar and does not grant access to private members.

In Java, this concept is not directly available. While you can achieve similar behavior using methods or passing objects explicitly, Java lacks the syntactic sugar provided by Kotlin's receivers. For example, in Kotlin, we can define extension functions or use lambdas with receivers, where the receiver becomes the implicit context within the block of code. This allows for more concise and readable code, as we can interact with the receiver object seamlessly within the function or lambda.

A receiver in Kotlin establishes a context when we define it. By defining a receiver within a lambda or a function, the receiver can be accessed as if it were within the object. This helps us to avoid explicit references; therefore, we will have cleaner and less repetitive code, meaning we will be able to access the methods and properties as we normally do in objects, but without needing to use the name of the object or the word this.

Receivers in Kotlin are a versatile feature that can be used in multiple contexts, such as the following:

- Extension functions   
- Lambda with receivers   
- Scope functions   
Property delegates   
- DSL builders   
- Extension properties   
- Objects with receivers   
- Inline functions   
- Interfaces   
Type aliases

The concept of receivers allows us to define a specific context within a function or lambda, enabling direct access to the properties and methods of an object without explicitly referencing it. This principle remains consistent across various contexts in Kotlin, making it unnecessary to redefine the concept for every use case.

In this chapter, we will focus on two key contexts where receivers are particularly useful: lambdas and in extension functions. These examples will demonstrate how receivers enhance readability and flexibility in Kotlin code.

To explain the concept of a receiver further, it is an object on which methods can be called and properties accessed within the body of a function, as if the function were a method of that object. A receiver allows us to interact with the object directly, often without explicitly referencing its name. For example, we commonly use the keyword this to refer to the current object in a context, but a receiver allows us to achieve this seamlessly, often without even needing this.

As mentioned earlier, receivers can be implemented in different elements, but for the purposes of this chapter, we will focus on extension functions and lambdas to demonstrate their practical applications.

```kotlin
    return builder.build()
} 
```

Modified buildMenu signature: We changed the type of the init lambda in buildMenu from (MenuBuilder) -> Unit to MenuBuilder.() -> Unit. Instead of passing builder as an argument, we call init directly on builder, allowing MenuBuilder to be the receiver within the lambda:

```txt

// After  
fun buildMenu(init: MenuBuilder.) -> Unit): List<MenuItem> 
```

As you can see, instead of passing builder as an argument to init, we now call init directly on builder:

```txt

init builder)  
// After  
builder.init() 
```
